utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Toma Fila, I appear with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic in the defence of my client, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic. MILENKO MILINKOVIC (continued).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Dokmanovic? Thank you. Before we proceed, may I draw to your attention a note which I received from the interpreters via the Registrar, where they rightly point out that, whenever a witness is provided with a document and is going to read out a document, the interpreters also need to have a copy of the document. Otherwise, their job becomes too demanding and too difficult. So, could you make an effort, whenever a document is read out by a party or by one of the witnesses, to provide in advance a copy of that document to the interpreters. Thank you so much. Let us continue with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Petrovic will continue, but I have to tell the court about something -- I complained to Mr. Niemann today, too. We as the defence, as you have seen for yourselves, are doing our very best to bring in witnesses. There is some kind of rule in this court that visas are issued to witnesses one day in advance. I spent two or three hours yesterday talking to the Dutch embassy in Belgrade, the secretary and in different ways. They are not working on Monday and today they work only until 2 p.m. And they said that if visa permits are not issued by the Tribunal by 10 o'clock this morning, they are not going to issue visas to these people unless they get these necessary papers. This way we are going to ruin three working days. I do not want to be dramatic -- I want to thank you first and foremost for granting safe conduct to these witnesses, but I do not know what to do. I wish to suggest the following: if these papers are not issued by 10 a.m. this morning, could visas be provided to these people, at Schipol airport? One of the witnesses is supposed to arrive tomorrow and the rest are supposed to arrive on Sunday. Otherwise, I do not know what we are going to do on Monday. What I am trying to say is that the defence is not to be blamed for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am not very clear about one particular point. You see the visa permits must be issued by the Tribunal -- do you mean requests for visas by the Dutch authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is not Croat authorities, it is Belgrade Serbia, still, thank God. I did not want to tire you -- the Tribunal requests visas from the Dutch Foreign Ministry. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the embassy in Belgrade that approval has been given at the request of the Tribunal, that these witnesses be granted visas for the duration of the trial. For example, those people who will be leaving tomorrow have all obtained visas until 30 April, when we are supposed to complete this particular portion of the trial, because we do not know exactly how long it will last, et cetera. So, if the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands, from The Hague, does not send approval to the embassy by 10 a.m. this morning, the embassy is not going to issue visas to these people and that is why I am saying the following: if it is impossible to do this until 10 a.m. today, that they could get visas at Schipol. This is what happened to the witnesses who were coming in when I was denying the legality of Mr. Dokmanovic's arrest, so perhaps we could act in the same way now as we did then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, I did not refer to the Croat authorities -- it was probably an interpretation. I am aware that the visas should be sent to Belgrade -- I know that. I wonder whether the Registrar could give us some explanation. I fully agree with Mr. Fila. I hope that all the necessary measures will be adopted, so that either the -- I assume that the request for visas have been issued by our Tribunal. Our problem is that the Dutch authorities should be asked to act immediately, or at least to provide the visas -- I fully agree with you. I wonder whether the Registrar could give us any information in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is usually a task of the Victim and Witness Unit, and we have not heard any problem from them. They have not informed us that there was a problem, so at this moment I cannot say any more than that I can ask the Victim and Witness Unit if they can contact the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could send a note to the head of the unit to impress upon them the importance of acting as soon as possible, by 10 o'clock, or in such a way that they can get visas at the airport. It is crucial, it is very important. I agree with Mr. Fila, we cannot agree to waste three days. Actually, may I take this opportunity to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Bos should not think that I hold anything against him. I know you have done your best and this has been sent from here, so the problem is not in the Tribunal really. The problem is that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not send the necessary papers or approval to Belgrade. To be quite clear -- I am not holding anything against you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we are all aware that even here in the Netherlands there is some red tape in the bureaucracy of various ministries, so sometimes things are slow. May I take this opportunity to ask Mr. Fila whether he feels that today we could hear not only Mr. Milinkovic but also the other two witnesses who are scheduled for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I hope we can finish, depending on the Prosecutor, of course. Could you then resume your examination? . Examination-in-chief by MR. PETROVIC (continued).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we adjourned at the point when you were explaining how the army attempted to get into Borovo Selo on 2 May. Could you please continue from that point? Why had the army set out at all towards Borovo Selo, with what objective?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope I can be heard now. Your Honour, I shall continue. To the best of my recollection, I was saying that the tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army had passed by a place where I was -- this was between Borovo and Borovo Selo. After a call was made from the MUP to tell the people who were blocking the road in' front of the tanks, because the MUP people were surrounded -- the MUP people who had attacked Borovo Selo. After that, I went back to Vukovar. There was quite a bit of commotion there -- many meetings were held. All those who it thought could contribute to the passive indication was assembled there. At one point, I remember Mr. Dzaja phoned me. We were talking about what could be done further, and he asked me whether I would not express my condolences to him, because of the deaths of 19 of his people and I said something to the effect that he had sent them to their death himself, because I had been warning him for days not to resort to force. First they said it was 19 people who were killed and then, afterwards, the official record said 12 or 13. Obviously, not all the MUP numbers were reported. I can only suppose why. At any rate, there were several versions that were in circulation. This was a turning point. This attack on Borovo Selo practically meant the beginning of the civil war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please explain the role of the Yugoslav People's Army in these events in Borovo Selo and immediately afterwards, what was actually the role of the Federal army at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was asked to intervene and to prevent the conflict and it intervened only in the following way: they came in APCs to Borovo Selo and evacuated the MUP members who were surrounded. Many of them were surrounded, so it is difficult to imagine what would have happened had the army not come in and evacuated them. Otherwise, during those days, after 2 May, there were many armed conflicts and the army was often invited by the Serbs, but also by the HDZ, or, rather, the police. On several occasions, the police asked the army to intervene when their people were surrounded in various situations. The army -- the Yugoslav People's Army throughout this period until the end of July while I was still in Vukovar -- exclusively intervened in that way. They separated the warring parties in every specific case of excess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify who invited the army on 2 May, because some of that remained unclear -- as you said yesterday, a phone call was made from the office of the President of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I phoned the army, although many people were accusing Mr. Dokmanovic, that he was the one who had called the army in. First, he was accused by the Serbs because they thought that the army should not be called in, because they thought that if they were already attacking, that there should be no separation between the parties that were fighting, so there were many accusations levelled against Mr. Dokmanovic, but he was not the one who invited the army to intervene -- I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I understand the interpreters did not get the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us summarise events in Borovo Selo. Let us briefly summarise them. How did they end, the events in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, I went to Borovo Selo -- that day it was impossible -- and I tried to reconstruct the sequence of events, so I talked to quite a few witnesses. Among other people, I talked to a lady called Ljubica, who was a clerk at the PTT and the post office was in the same building where the local community offices were, where the fighting actually started. According to the statements of several witnesses, at one point in time, in front of the local community premises where the defence headquarters were, a car that was moving very fast stopped abruptly -- it was an Opel -- and Dzaja, together with a few policemen, jumped out of it and they opened fire on this building where the defence headquarters of Borovo Selo was. They did not know at that time there was no-one in the building -- in front of the building, there was only a man who was a guard. At that point, he was sitting on the steps with his army in his lap, but his army was disassembled. I know this particular detail, because Mr. Podlovzoric and Mr. Dzugic, two of my employees at the post office, they were passing by and they told me about this detail. He was killed on the spot, and some passers-by were wounded. I heard four or five witnesses say the same thing, that for the first five or 10 minutes no-one responded to this fire that was opened by the police. After this car, three more cars stopped -- the two jeeps and the traffic vehicle that I mentioned, in which the ZNG members were, and behind them two buses full of armed ZNG members. They all got out of these vehicles and started firing and I repeat, all the witnesses said that, for the first five or 10 minutes, there was no response from the other side. After five or 10 minutes, however, the other side started shooting back. The Croat policemen got into the local community building -- that is where an outpatient clinic was -- and they held the people who happened to be there as hostages, and also the people who happened to be in a nearby cafe. The people who happened to be in the street then during the fighting, which was getting worse and worse, including Croat policemen, they were getting hit as there was a lot of shooting from the roofs of buildings that were nearby. I saw the buses, which the Croat policemen took to get to Borovo Selo, and I saw a lot of food that was not fully eaten -- pieces of sausage, bread and also cigarettes that were not fully smoked. Obviously, this all came abruptly. Apparently, they were told that they were going out for an exercise -- not for an all-out armed attack. So, after a short period of time, these policemen were surrounded. That is why they insisted from the police station that the army should be let in. When the army came in on APCs, although there was still shooting at that time, they got into this zone and they took the surrounded Croat policemen and took them away in these APCs. I mentioned Matkovic, who was head of the special forces of the Croat police. On that occasion, he kissed the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army -- rather, an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army -- and thanked him in this way for saving his life. I heard about it later, both from Matkovic, and from this officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest the following. I think that we have clarified events in Borovo Selo on 2 May. Immediately after that, in the assembly of the Municipality of Vukovar a meeting was held where some high federal officials were present, too. Could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those days, there was lively political activity going on, because efforts were made to pacify the situation and, among other things, at the initiative of Mr. Dokmanovic, a meeting was convened at his office and high federal officials were invited and high officials of Croatia. Mr. Markovic, the Federal Prime Minister was there, Boljkovac was there and his associates on behalf of the Government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What office did they hold then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boljkovac was, if I am not mistaken, Minister of the Interior; Brovet was there from the Yugoslav People's Army -- a general -- I am not sure which one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brovet was, at that time, Deputy Minister for defence -- Federal Minister for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, a delegation was there and the meeting was chaired by Mr. Dokmanovic and efforts were made to see how this situation, which actually meant an outbreak of a civil war, could be overcome. Unfortunately, already at that point, every side had its own view of the problem. The Croat side said that people lost their lives. At one point in time, I said that it was a great pity that so many were killed, but that I cannot help thinking that they were sent to their deaths on purpose, so that this could contribute to the objective of national homogenisation. Mr. Boljkovac did not say anything in response to that. I still think to this day that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, I wish to show you a document, D6, and could you please tell us what kind of document this is (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I speak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document which was produced at the initiative of Mr. Dokmanovic. At that time, the situation was extremely complex, extremely difficult, and it was wished to overcome this situation. This was ethnic tension. Ethnic tensions were on the rise and thus an effort was being made to ease these tensions and to find a peaceful solution. Mr. Dokmanovic gave a proposal and this resolution was sent through the Municipal Assembly to the best of my recollection to the Government of the Republic of Croatia and to Yugoslav institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these events in Borovo Selo, can you tell us whether, in the town of Vukovar, there were cases of pressure brought to bear against the Serbs; were Serbs expelled from the area; did any of them move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to give a more precise answer to this question, I shall only say in a few words what the chronology of these pressures was from the very outset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us only a few impressive examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few examples of this kind, so I am only going to point out those in which I took part directly, or if I heard about them from the protagonists of the actual events directly. It is very difficult to explain how this happened gradually. Life used to be normal there, but, through constant pressure, a psychosis developed among people. After all, people were used to living together over there. Although this was a multi-ethnic community, there were not only Croats and Serbs living there, but also members of many other nationalities, ethnic groups. But, through the gradual action taken by individuals, this psychosis was gradually created. It is very difficult to explain this in words and it is difficult to grasp, for people who had not lived through it. If I had not lived through it myself, I really could not understand it, either. It started with very small provocations, for example, the monument dedicated to the Partisans near Bobota was first destroyed. This happened some time before the elections. Then other provocations started. There was an inscription in the Cyrillic script on the Municipal Assembly and somebody shot at it during the night and, during another night, somebody had taken it down and nothing happened afterwards. The police did not even carry out an investigation, but even if they did carry out an investigation, they never submitted a report to that effect and no-one was ever punished for that. These excesses became worse and worse and, during 1991, it is not only buildings that were shot at. I am only going to mention one example -- there were very many. A worker of mine, Ms. Skorupan, had a few bursts of gunfire fired at her house during the night and she told me about it in the morning. After that, some people started shooting from cars that drove through villages with a majority Serb population and, also, cars drove by with Croat chessboard flags and they would make a lot of noise in the process, but then, during May, they also started shooting from these cars, and also some time in April a car that was moving through the village of Brsadin, there were people in this car who started shooting from it and two young men who happened to be in the street were wounded as a result of that. In Borovo Selo, even before 2 May, in the direction of Dalj, two rifle grenades were fired, I think. I am not very good with weapons but I think these were rifle grenades, so all of this together gave rise to tensions. First, people felt uneasy, then this turned into fear and, finally, this also turned into resoluteness on the part of many people that they should oppose this kind of terror. Regularly, both Mr. Dokmanovic and I would go to the very spot where these things would happen and we would try to calm people down, so that the whole situation could become more peaceful and not turn into a civil war after all. This shelling up to 2 May was, for the most part, rifle shooting and hitting of buildings and creating a climate of unrest. This feeling of total uncertainty that your very existence was being threatened and this was a very horrendous feeling, and people began to feel that they had to defend themselves in some way. However, after 2 May, quite openly, attacks were launched both on the Serb property and on Serbs -- attacks were made on Serb lives. Many buildings were rooted from the ground. First of all, these were cafe bars, the Karolina and Sarajka and other cafe bars, there were quite a number of them, but people were being shot at as well. At the beginning of May, in the village of Sotin which is right next to Vukovar, from a moving car there was gunfire, people were shot at and Mr. Nad was killed -- he was a member of the SDS, and the man next to him was wounded. In the village of Brsadin, once again in May, from a silo where the snipers were located of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Croatia, a young man was killed in the village itself. During those days, my wife was shot at from those same silos. They had gone to collect the workers working in the fields, about one to one and a half kilometres away from the silos, and so quite openly not only was Serb property being threatened, but Serb lives as well. At the same time, the army stepped in exclusively in cases of attacks of these kinds, either where there were conflicting situations where the Serbs were jeopardised or where the Croats were endangered, but, in the second half of May, it became highly -- life in Vukovar became highly uncertain and precarious and many people from Vukovar took their families out of the environs of Vukovar and began to leave. I personally had to move my children in the room facing the street, because there was shooting throughout the night, usually after midnight, and it was not safe to sleep in any of the rooms of our apartment looking out on to the street. Somewhere around the end of May, the psychosis was such that people began to leave the -- Serbs began to leave Vukovar en masse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Vukovar and what were the circumstances governing your departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I evacuated my family from Vukovar at the beginning of July. I will tell you about those events. What happened was the following: already, at the end of June, it became very difficult, almost impossible, to continue to live in Vukovar. There were explosions, shelling, shootings, killings, every night, and the people began to leave Vukovar en masse. When the members of the Zenga killed Jakovljevic, nicknamed Rakijica, in his home -- this was somewhere at the end of June -- a few days before that, I met him -- the PTT building and the VELEPROMET department store were close by, so we met at his office -- he was the head for sportswear and he said that he was being threatened by Mercep's people, and that he had to surrender this sports weaponry and he said he would not, but he would surrender it to the army. He was killed at the threshold of his house when the members of the Zenga surrounded his house and they just shot him. This was the reason why we asked that the Government intervene and I asked Mr. Mato Arlovic, who was the deputy from Osijek in the Parliament, to convene a meeting with Sime Dodan. Sime Dodan was the Minister of Internal Affairs. This was his second day in the post and he later called himself the War Minister and, so on 3 July, in the morning, Mr. Bosnjakovic, the deputy from Vukovar and myself, went by car -- I took Rade Gojic -- a relative of mine, who one day previously, somewhere around 4 p.m., for four hours, a group of over 30 members of the Zenga specialist units had maltreated him in his home. They stormed the house at about 4 p.m., they searched for arms and they maltreated them for more than four hours. They found no weaponry and, in a panic, him and his wife came to our house. My wife took the car and fetched them. I took him with me on that particular morning. Let me just say that his house was shot at from somewhere between May and June -- I think it was on 31 May during the night -- from a vehicle which Mr. Gojic was able to identify. Several minutes later they began shooting at his sister's house. He was once again able to identify this vehicle, and it belonged to one of Mercep's close associates. This means that, on the morning of 3 July, via Brsadin, Pazjadin and Bobota, I went in the direction of -- Rade Gojic remained in Bobata -- he was very grateful for having his life saved. In Osijek we picked up Mr. Mato Arlovic, and in Zagreb, in the Parliament, although the meeting was convened for 10, we had to wait a long time and we had occasion to talk to one of Tudjman's associates, councillors, I forget his name, but I remember he was a very reasonable man, one of the rare men who showed a great deal of reason. We told him what was happening and what Mercep was doing in Osijek and Glavas and he was very depressed to hear the news, but the impression I gained was that he was not only depressed because of what he heard, but that he knew something more. Somewhere around 2 or 3 p.m., Mr. Dodan received us, and I let Mr. Bosnjakovic and Mr. Mato Arlovic present the facts so that I would not be said to have been prejudiced. When I felt that they had not presented sufficient arguments to bear out the truth of what was happening in Vukovar and Osijek, I put in a few words myself. The meeting went on for quite some time, because Mr. Dodan was called away to headquarters several times. The Cabinet of the MUP was directly next to the Parliament building. At one point he said quite openly that he knew about them, but that he cannot do anything about the situation, because their conduct would directly lead to civil war. He said that there was no way in which he could get rid of them, except to kill them, and that he was not allowed to do this and to quote him, he said: "Precisely today we were told that unless we fulfil the promises we made -- the pledge that we made, we would receive a bullet ourselves." I must say that, at that particular moment, I did not understand who the "they" were exactly, but I came to realise later on that this referred to the people who brought them to power. He also told me that nobody could guarantee my own personal safety in Croatia, and I was resigned and depressed and left his office, his Cabinet, in that manner, and downstairs in the hallway I saw Mr. Degoricija and, instead of a greeting, he just said to me, "Milinkovic, we were very naive, both of us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you finally leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I finish what I was saying? It was only at that point that I fully realised who the individuals were who had brought them to power. After that, I returned to Vukovar and, two or three days later, I took my family away -- it was some time around the beginning of July, I came back once at the end of the July to Vukovar in a Combi, and that was my last sojourn in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your talk with the investigator for the defence was not your first contact with the Tribunal, was it? Would you tell us about this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1995 -- I contacted the Tribunal at the beginning of 1996 and, in the course of 1996, with Tatjana Termacic, I presented my views and opinions. Mr. Dokmanovic came to me at that time and, together, we had talks with Ms. Tatjana Termacic and decided that both of us would give the Tribunal statements on everything that happened in Vukovar from the pre-electoral activities to the final tragic days and Mr. Dokmanovic decided, with Ms. Termacic, to give this same statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, would you just help us with this, please? The D6 memorandum you referred to, the resolution on resolving inter-ethnic tensions; it appears that there is no date on the English version, but looking at the back, at least in my copy, it appears that the original seems to be dated 23 February. What I was wanting your help on is the date -- is that the date of the resolution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 23 February, that is when this resolution was published in the Vukovar gazette, that is to say, the official gazette of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, that is 23 February and I imagine that a few days previous to that it was actually passed in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, my name is Clint Williamson, I am one of the attorneys for the Office of the Prosecutor. You indicated a moment ago you had this meeting with Ms. Termacic in the latter part of 1996 and early 1997 in order to give a witness statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of 1996, as far as I recall, it was -- on several occasions, I think it took us five or six days to provide this witness statement, but it was in 1996, before Mr. Dokmanovic was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was the statement taken down in the Serb language reviewed by you and then signed by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show you this document, which I am going to mark with the next Prosecutor's exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 193.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Prosecutor's exhibit 193. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would you examine that and tell me if that appears to be your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And if a copy can be provided to the defence as well? You had a chance to review that statement and you placed your signature on it, indicating that it was correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the document was drawn up on several occasions, which can be seen on page number 1 -- we started on 18 October and completed on 13 May 1997. The final document was not printed out and I did not read the printed version, but I did read the previous version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you received a copy of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Ms. Termacic said that I could not receive a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to now offer the English translation of this, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 193

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Handed). The statement that you gave to the defence on 24 February 1998, and which has been tendered as a defence exhibit, I believe it is number 31, if you can help me with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The statement that you gave to the defence is very similar to the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996. In fact, with the exception of two brief paragraphs, the defence statement appears to track portions of the earlier statement verbatim; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there is one truth, then it is difficult to have two testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But, to the point where every word is exact for seven pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of our work on making this statement, from 18 October to 13 May 1997, which means on several occasions this statement was drawn up on a series of occasions, I had a copy of the material as it stood until that particular point, and when we drew up the statement, part of the material was used in continuing my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But the defence statement, however, omits significant portions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And giving this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not enough time -- at least, I did not have enough time to give a complete statement straight away, because this was done over a period of several days and, to repeat something -- giving something to the Tribunal once again, I did not want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So did you provide the materials that you had received already from the Office of the Prosecutor to the defence -- there is nothing wrong with that -- I am just asking if that is what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the separate papers -- I did not have time to give the complete version, so I gave separate papers. The making of the statement lasted a long time, so I did not want to run the risk of entering into repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honours. At this point I would just point out that, on the Prosecutor's exhibit 193A, the English translation of this, we have indicated where the defence statement tracks the Prosecutor's statement by the addition of black lines. I am sure you have already had a chance to read through the defence exhibit, so these portions are duplicative and it is only those portions not included with the black lines that do not appear in the defence statement. Mr. Milinkovic, you speak of various provocations by the Croat side at places at Plitvice and Borovo Selo, but I believe yesterday you said the final crux, as you described it, in terms of deterioration of the situation was the adoption of the Croat constitution in December 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction that the consequence -- that is to say, everything that happened was a consequence of the strategic goal of the HDZ to realise the function of statehood at all cost and actions of this kind by the HDZ, and as it represented the Croat authorities, then via it, all the consequences were the result of that strategic decision. I said that there were several key turning points, because of which the Serbs in Croatia lost their trust in the Croat authorities. It started de facto from the petty provocations, via the Plitvice events and the turning point was the civil war in Borovo Selo, but I also said that the Croat authorities showed more tolerance and more time -- had it had more time and understanding and had it shown more tolerance, it would have had the Serbs as loyal citizens of Croatia -- had it done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Plitvice occurred at the end of March 1991 -- I believe 31 March 1991 -- and Borovo Selo happened on 2 May 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, have you ever heard of events which occurred in the Knin area in August 1990 which were referred to as the "log revolution"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I did not have any direct contacts with those people, but several talks with representatives from that region. I know that they set up barriers along the roads, having been provoked by the decisions made by the Croat authorities, but what actually took place, I do not really know. I only presented some of the data of the events that I either took part in personally, referring to the Vukovar area, or where I had received information from the actual protagonists in the events themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But do you know enough about this to say if this was a situation where the Serbs had blocked off roads in the Krajina area and were not allowing Croats to pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the roads were blocked, but I do not know the true reason as to why this happened. I do not believe that somebody would just block off roads for no special reason, but I do know what it was like in the municipality of Vukovar, and that quite definitely it was not the Serbs that rebelled and they did not resort to armed rebellion through a whim of theirs; it was a necessary act to protect themselves from the organised terror that was directed towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one other question in relation to this in Knin. Do you know enough about the region to tell me if the road that passes through Knin is the main route from Zagreb to the coast -- to Split, the second largest city in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I said a moment ago -- my testimony is restricted exclusively to the Vukovar municipality, where I myself was personally involved and where I had quite clear-cut data -- exact data. In answer to your question, I can say I think it is the main road, but it is not the only road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So blocking this route between Zagreb and Split, the second largest city in Croatia, would have a significant impact on the Croat economy, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you say so -- I take that to be correct. The question is what the causes and what the effect is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Would the Prosecutor stick to the testimony of Mr. Milinkovic? The events in and around Knin is not something he has personal knowledge of, but something he learned from the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I might respond to this, the witness testified about Plitvice which is also in the area of Knin, and obviously he has exhibited some knowledge of that. He is putting forward assertions these were provocations started by the Croat side and that these started in March and May 1991. I am merely challenging these assertions and this is the purpose of cross-examination, to test what this witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. On the other hand, the witness has repeatedly stated that he has no personal knowledge and no personal information of what happened in Krajina. I wonder whether you could move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Let me ask this -- August of 1990 was four months before the adoption of the Croat constitution, was it not -- in December 1990? It was a good seven or eight months before Plitvice and Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: August of 1990 is four months before December of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And seven or eight months before March and May of 1991, when Plitvice and Borovo Selo occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That was the question, is it not before that? I believe you have answered the question. In relation to Plitvice, you expressed an opinion yesterday that this was an intentional provocation by the Croats and you have repeated that assertion today; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I expressed the view that before every meeting of the SABOR Croat Parliament, an excessive situation took place and it is difficult to believe they took place just by chance prior to a parliamentary meeting. I had the opinion that this was done consciously, that these excessive situations were consciously created so that the Parliament could then discuss the issue and blame it on the Serbs and this could then serve the purposes of national homogenisation. You must bear in mind one fact after the multi-Party elections in Croatia, many Croats were not in favour of the extremist policy waged by the HDZ. The HDZ was fully aware of this quite obviously, and to achieve its strategic goal and to win over most of the population, in my view, he wanted to use these excessive situations and to blame the Serbs, to create the view, with the people, that it was the Serbs who were responsible for the situation and then to win over those Croats who were not quite convinced -- who were not convinced at the beginning, to win them over for their strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The whole incident came about in Plitvice when the Croats established a police station there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have this information from the newspapers alone and it is difficult for me and neither do I wish to speak about something which I do not have tested data and facts for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You say you know absolutely nothing about the facts of what happened at Plitvice, but you have formed a conclusion that this was a provocation by the Croats and that you were asserting that to the court; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I maintain that this was part of the overall provocations which were created. After these events I asked that, as soon as possible, the perpetrators be brought to justice, if they were responsible, if they were guilty, that they should answer for their acts. I have always advocated the fact that the instruments of the State must be implemented equally on a footing of equality to all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you have no knowledge of the facts as to how this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know the last part, that Mr. Savic told me about, after he was released from prison, some 10 days after he had been arrested, several interventions were made on his behalf and he was brought in black and blue -- obviously, he had really been beaten up, and he said that, as one of the protagonists, that he and Hadzic were asleep at the hotel when the conflict broke out and they did not have any weapons and they were not informed what was going on, so I know about this from what Mr. Savic had said and he said that they had not caused this intervention in any way, because they were spending the night at the hotel in Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Savic is a Serb that you talked to and, as you said, was one of the protagonists and this is your sole basis of information, that is, his version of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information that carried more weight, to my mind, were those that I had witnessed myself and experienced myself and those that I got from people who were direct participants in the events concerned, and I believe Mr. Savic to be a reasonable man and therefore I took this to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated after Plitvice the Serbs erected barricades on roads coming into and out of their villages in the Vukovar municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. This happened in Borovo Selo, but it is also true that this happened when a group of policemen, in the village itself, provoked a group of young men -- I do not know, perhaps the young men had incited this in another way -- I do not know, but the police patrol asked for reinforcement from Vukovar. A few police cars came after that. According to the stories of the witnesses, the participants in the events, there was some quarrelling, even skirmishes, but then, when weapons were drawn, the local people disarmed the police, so you never really know what came first -- the provocation or response to a provocation -- although I always advocated the following, that provocation should not be responded to by another provocation, but I always advocated democratic methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was not this an illegal act of putting up barricades around villages and blocking roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, this was an illegal act, but do you think that it was a legal act to shoot in that same village? On the other side, towards Dalj, to use explosives, to shoot at buildings and that is exactly what happened before that. The barricades were a consequence of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And the barricades around the Croat areas went up only after the Serbs had erected barricades in their villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some villages of the Vukovar municipality -- I cannot say about others -- like in Berak, the barricades were erected along parallel lines, around the Serb and Croat villages. It is difficult to say which came first and which came afterwards, but the fact remains that this psychosis of insecurity and safety was systematically being created and this was initiated by the representatives of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I call your attention to the statement you gave to the Prosecutor -- I am not sure of the page in the Serb version. In the English version it appears on page 21 paragraph 3, and to quote this, it says: "The incident in Plitvice caused a spontaneous reaction and people organised themselves and set up village guards and road blocks in Serb villages. The road blocks usually consisted of agricultural machines. The road blocks then started appearing in the Croat villages and then in the town itself." Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is just about right. The barricades first appeared in Borovo Selo, but practically on the next day in other villages -- in Croat villages, too. But I said that that barricade was a consequence of these two events -- police provocations in the village and shooting with explosives at buildings in the village. It was exceptionally difficult to explain to people that the fact that their buildings were being shot at and that they were being provoked, was of a peaceful nature and it is difficult for people who advocate such solutions to enjoy any kind of authority among these people. That is why Mr. Dokmanovic and I had long lost our authority among the Serbs and we were practically considered to be traitors among the Serbs, because we were in favour of peaceful solutions and we wanted to do everything possible in order to avoid the outbreak of a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Let us move to Borovo Selo, which you discussed in some detail. You say the police chief in Vukovar told you that two of his men were missing in Borovo Selo, and is it not true that two Croat policemen were being held by the Serbs in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaja told me that these were two policemen of his, and it turned out that these policemen were actually from the Osijek police station. Borovo Selo is under the jurisdiction of the Vukovar police station, or the Vinkovski-Vukovar-Zupanja police station at that point, so the question was why these policemen were there anyway? According to the information that I received subsequently, according to one piece of information, rather, there were three of these policemen. They drove in a car through Borovo Selo, so there were not any barricades then, because they came from the direction of Dalj. On several occasions we managed to reach agreement to have the barricades removed, but, as I said yesterday, usually only a day later another provocation would follow, just as what happened in Borovo Selo and these policemen wanted to take down the Serb flag or the Yugoslav flag -- I am not too sure any more -- which was on the outskirts of the village, and then there was shooting again and then these two policemen were caught -- I think they were also wounded -- and then they were taken to a hospital somewhere to Serbia, I believe -- I cannot remember, I am not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that Borovo Selo is in the Vukovar police jurisdiction. The town of Dalj is in the Osijek police jurisdiction, is it not -- it is in the Osijek municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So, if policemen were going from Dalj to Vukovar, they would pass through Borovo Selo; correct -- on the most direct route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not wish to give information here which I cannot corroborate and for which I do not have proof, but it was said that they were sent to start provocations and that this was at the orders of Mr. Glavas, but what I am saying here now is only what I heard from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am asking you a very simple question -- the most direct route from Dalj to Vukovar passes through Borovo Selo; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you think it is unreasonable for a police force to try to mount an operation to rescue two wounded officers who were being held captive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very difficult to understand, from this time distance and also from this particular context, the psychosis that was created there and then. I witnessed peaceful citizens, because most of the citizens on the territory of the municipality of Vukovar, both Serbs and Croats were peaceful citizens, turn into people who were resolute to defend their own lives and the lives of their families. For days I had been warning Mr. Dzaja and Mr. Matkovic and Mr. Sredoselac that by no means should any resort to force be made, and if you recall, I said yesterday that, although I had by then fully lost all credibility among citizens of Serb ethnic origin, I offered to go there myself and to see what was going on. Political means of resolving something are always preferable to resorting to force. As far as I know, on that very same day, these two men were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the police officers were killed on 2 May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received information that they were released the very same day, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As I understand your testimony from yesterday, and again today, you stated that the Croat police more or less attacked Borovo Selo and that the villagers were caught by surprise; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack on Borovo Selo was carried out from several directions by the police headquarters for Vinkovski, Vukovar and Zupanja under the command of Mr. Dzaja and I said that, from what I could see, from an Opel vehicle -- it was the Opel vehicle in which Bosnjak was that did this, and two other jeeps and two other buses and I also heard there was another vehicle which had been lost along the way, so there were quite a few policemen involved -- we can assess that at this point -- and, from the direction of Dalj, Borovo Selo was attacked from the Osijek police station and this was under the command of Mr. Kir, who was later killed. It was being said in the SABOR, the Croat Parliament, that his death was actually a result of his opposition to that kind of attack, and, also, he was not to be blamed that yet another attack was launched from the same site and that is why the village organised its defence. How many people took part in this? I do not know. According to various information, there were even more policemen on that side and, according to many witness statements -- I do not have any personal knowledge of this -- many more people were killed there. But Croatia was not prepared to make this public. However, in the Croat Parliament we heard that Minister Babac, Minister of the Judiciary, had some of his favourite people killed there, because they were called Babac's favourites, because it was alleged that he had released people from prison and allowed them to take part in such attacks. I have no personal knowledge of this, but this is what was being said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And so it is your contention that this was the local people of Borovo Selo who organised their defence in the face of this attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally cannot assert who all the participants were. I would come to Borovo Selo. I knew quite a few of them, but I saw at least five or six people whom I did not know. I do not know who they were. I just know they were not from the village. However, it is impossible that it was only someone else who took part in this defence -- according to the information I received while collecting witness statements a few days after this event, the defence was predominantly organised by the villagers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Serb paramilitary groups from Serbia being involved in the defence of Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that I saw five or six people, and I would come often to Borovo Selo -- five or six people I did not know -- so I thought they were volunteers or someone else, but I really do not know exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know who Vojislav Seselj is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And he was not from Borovo Selo, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In fact, he is from Belgrade, is he not -- or he lives in Belgrade now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where he was born but now he does live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at the time in 1991, he was living in Belgrade, was not he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj led a paramilitary group that called themselves the "Chetniks", did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This name "Chetniks" is derived from history. It was the Croat media that first called them Chetniks, so then people got used to using that word, but it is my profound conviction that there were not very many such people. There were very few of them. As I said in Borovo Selo, I only saw five or six people who came from somewhere else. It is impossible that so many of them managed to hide, that I could not see them. I was there almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But in relation to Mr. Seselj, he referred to himself as a Chetnik Duke, did he not, or a vojvodno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is his right, I do not want to enter into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show a brief video clip. It is taken from Radio Television Belgrade. It is on "The Death of Yugoslavia". If it can start please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is in relation to Borovo Selo -- I am not sure exactly. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then there is one other clip which comes right after this, if that can be shown as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, let us take note of the fact that these are video clips made in Belgrade -- I think we will agree on that, that this was shot in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, the speaking part there was shot in Belgrade and the -- it is the continuation of the interview with Mr. Seselj. We have tried as much as possible to take out the commentary which is provided. There is one brief part of commentary in this as well. If this can start -- this is in Borovo Selo itself, the Serbs in the Vukovar suburb seized two Croat policemen. The Croats hit back. Two buses of heavily armed Croat police drove confidently into the Serb strong hold, straight into an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, you have heard the comments of Mr. Seselj here, and he seems to have a lot of knowledge about what happened at Borovo Selo. Does that indicate that the Croats, to you, seemed to be launching some kind of a surprise attack, driving right down the main street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What certain politicians resort to for the sake of their political marketing is something that I do not wish to comment upon. What Mr. Zezey said is really his problem, but, in my statement, I mentioned the statements of people who were on the spot at that particular point in time. I said what Ms. Ljubica said, who was an employee of the post office. At that point, she was in this building -- it is the same building. I mentioned what she said and at least another four or five witnesses, whom I heard a day later, that is to say, while their impressions were still very fresh. They all said that the Opel that Mr. Bosnjak raced out of was the first vehicle to come to an abrupt halt and, without any warning, from that vehicle, they started shooting at this building. This guard on the steps of that building was killed. I heard that he was not from Borovo Selo, that is true. But, also, all the witnesses agree on the following: for the first five or 10 minutes, nobody else had shot and no-one else had responded with gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These witnesses that you are all referring to were Serbs who lived in Borovo Selo; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one of the witnesses is unfortunately deceased -- Mr. Zugec -- he was a Croat by nationality and, two minutes before that event, he went by this guard, because, in the yard of that building we had a telephone exchange and he was a technician who worked at the telephone exchange, and only two minutes before this event he went by and he told me about it; that is to say, that both Serbs and Croats told me about it -- Mr. Zugec -- although I had personally intervened with Mr. Sredoselac that they should be released, but as he was getting out of Borovo Selo, he was beaten up by Croat policemen and they would not even let him show his documents to prove that he was a Croat. He was beaten up because he wore a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would it not have been illegal for armed paramilitary groups from the Republic of Serbia to be operating on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely illegal, but do you think that it is legal to shoot at people from a vehicle that is moving through the village? I told you that had a happened in the village of Brsadin. This happened before Borovo Selo -- two accidental passers-by were wounded. In Borovo Selo, also before 2 May, when I managed -- both Mr. Soskocanin and Mr. Sredoselac, to have them meet in Borovo Selo itself and when we agreed to have the road blocks removed and in the morning, traffic was resumed and on the very next day, people start shooting from a police vehicle at buildings in that village. I heard from Mr. Sredoselac that these were not his people, but they were wearing uniforms, so who were these people?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did not the legitimate police authorities of the Republic of Croatia have the right to try to enforce the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you call the law driving through the village and firing at buildings and everything around, I do not think that I can agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So it is your contention that these were just all one-sided incidents -- that the Croat police were going around terrorising Serb citizens in Vukovar everywhere, that none of this was caused by the Serbs at all, this is just a one-sided affair from the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am deeply convinced that, had there not been provocation on the part of the Croat authorities, had there been the necessary respect shown for the Serbs as citizens of Croatia, in a relatively short period of time Croatia, as a State, would have Serbs in Croatia as its loyal citizens. I say this with full conviction for the area in which I lived. I am quite certain that the beginning of the excesses did not come from the Serb side -- it is not my intention to defend anybody who is guilty, but I have seen so many events, I took part in so many events that I can say fully responsibly that, in that region, the excesses did not start from the Serbs and that is why I maintain, and this was the general conviction, that an answer to all these excessive situations and, later on, firing and killing, the answer was not an armed struggle but was a necessary act of self protection against organised terrorism or terror. This is borne out by all the facts that I have at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just one more question, your Honour, and then perhaps we can take the break. Would you characterise Mr. Zezey's paramilitary soldiers that were apparently running around the area, as moderates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not, and I am not talking about them. They are just a appendage of the climate that had been created. Had there not been the climate created by the Croat authorities, there would be no scope for the activities of these individuals who had appeared -- they would have nothing to do there. The question is of cause and effect, what the cause and effect is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think we can agree there were not a lot of Croats in Mr. Zezey's forces, can we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose you are right. I never talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be a good time for a recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you need more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I will need some additional time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (10.00 a.m.). (A short adjournment).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Williamson, may I ask the witness to try to be more concise in his answers -- to make an effort, if you can, try to be more concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think we need to correct one housekeeping matter. I spoke with Mr. Bos during the break. Apparently, we gave duplicative exhibit numbers to the witness statement that I provided. Rather than exhibit 193, that should actually be 194 and 194A, so I believe that clears it up, does it not, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you whether you could enquire about the dates of the tapes we saw this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It would be very important for us to know the dates, when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure exactly. I can try to determine this. These came from "The Death of Yugoslavia" series. We can see if we can make that determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution will agree -- at least I suppose it will -- I am not sure whether this is a good thing for me, in my favour, as the defence counsel, but I think it would be a good idea if you saw the whole tape, because it was neither filmed by the Prosecution nor by us, or Croats or Serbs but the English, the British, and if you agree, I think that it would be a good idea to show the whole tape. It is not a long one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is it, the whole tape? If it was a series --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I may respond to that? There were five programmes, which were each one hour in length. The first three deal largely with the build-up to the conflict and the conflict in Croatia, and the final two deal largely with Bosnia, so it would be approximately three hours in length, the portions that would be pertinent to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We do not have to see them here and now. You can see them later, segment by segment, or what is interesting for you. I think that it would be of use to you and I think that Prosecutor Williamson would agree that it would be beneficial for you to see it. We do not have to see it all together here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think we should see them here in court, at least the relevant parts. Judge Mumba would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: My worry is that that is a BBC videotape -- it is a media tape -- it is by journalists who put it together, to put up their story to show the world, is it not? It is totally different from say the Prosecution preparing their case. This is the problem. That is why we wanted the dates and also to be able to say whether or not this tape was shot during the incidents, or whether it is an edited one. Do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, entirely. This would be the only concern that we would have about the about showing these programmes. There are a number of interviews which take place, which are shown on the programme, which I think would be extremely helpful to the court. It is individuals who were in positions of authority speaking about what they did and what motivated them to do things, but I think your concern, Judge Mumba, is the fact of the commentary that goes with this, and how things are edited. So, it is perhaps a little bit tricky. There is certainly a lot of material on there that would be worthwhile and would help perhaps to clarify some of the issues before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, you testified earlier about what the role of the JNA was in May at Borovo Selo, and you said that you could only say what the role of the JNA was up until you left Vukovar, which was some time in July; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My complete testimony refers to the period up to the end of July, when I was in Vukovar for the last time, and when we mention the JNA, I speak about the JNA up to the end of July. Until that time, according to my knowledge, the army did not intervene in any other fashion than to separate the two conflicting sides -- although the army was shot at in Ilok in July -- it was shot at from the Croat armed forces, and I personally experienced an event at the end of May when the representatives of the federal SUP had a delegation to study the causes of the conflict and to calm them down -- they invited me to the garrison for talks to give my opinions. This talk was a rather lengthy one and around the garrison there were observers from the HDZ looking to see who was entering the garrison. We completed these discussions somewhere around midnight. The streets were completely empty. My house is the other side of town. In front of me there was a military jeep with an officer and two soldiers. Somewhere around the market place, which is in the centre of the town, I was passed by a Combi, and I saw the silhouettes of people in that vehicle and I thought there were some poles. When the doors opened and when these poles were targeted towards the jeep, the military vehicle, I realised that they were rifles, so I started to go faster, I put on my lights so that I could throw a light on to the vehicle between the jeep and my own car, and they did not open fire. But they did open the doors, the side doors, to shoot at the military vehicle. Because I had my head lights on them, they failed to do so. As we turned towards the Municipal Assembly building, I was stopped by uniformed civilians -- they were some kind of HDZ guard. They saw my parliamentary ID and let me through, but, as they saw that I had come to a stop, the military vehicle had come to a stop, whereas the Combi passed by and no shooting occurred on that particular occasion, but I was the direct witness and I believed that had I not shot my headlights at them, they would have opened fire on the army. They passed by immediately, because the HDZ patrol near the municipal building let them pass through, whereas they detained me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But my question, Mr. Milinkovic, was that you were not able to say what the army did after July; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. I want only to speak of events where I was a witness myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you -- try to give short answers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, you indicated in your statement to the Prosecutor, to Ms. Termacic, which has been marked as exhibit 194, on page 24, paragraph 1, that, when the HDZ heard that Slavko Dokmanovic had become a member of the Serb National Council, the open attacks against him became more intense. Do you know when he joined this organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just heard about this. I do not know exactly what period this was. It was in 1991, but I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You are not aware of exactly at what point he had joined the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But the period that you are talking about there, when you make that statement, this is around the time of the Borovo Selo incident, is it not? I am sorry, I know you do not have the statement in front of you and my references are in the English version rather than on the Serb version. You mentioned the date April 1991 in that same paragraph. You said: "When the HDZ heard that Slavko Dokmanovic had become a member of the Serb National Council, the open attacks against him became more intense and the intention was to have him replaced. When the Municipal Assembly gave him a vote of confidence and the HDZ realised they could do nothing that way, in April 1991, the HDZ Assemblyman Fekete submitted a request at a Municipal Assembly session for the Municipal Assembly to be dissolved." So this would have been prior to April 1991 when he joined the organisation and these threats ensued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what character the Serb National Council had, but I suppose it was in that period. As far as I recall, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You mention in the next paragraph, paragraph 2 on page 24 of the English version: "The Serb National Council was a body that was meant to represent Serb national interests and protect Serb human rights." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you consider this to be a moderate group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the information that I had, I think that at least what they said and their activities within that time were moderate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a book, which I am going to mark for identification as Prosecutor's exhibit 196. I am afraid I have only one copy of this book, but I would just ask, if you could look at this, and if you can read out the title of this book, please. (Handed). Can you read the title of this book, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The Serb National Council for Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem", Ilija Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the back of the book, there appears a brief bibliography of the author -- if you could read that out. As you read, I know there is a tendency to go more quickly, but could you read it more slowly so that the interpreters can keep up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Notes on the author: Ilija Petrovic was born on 6 September 1938 in Podgorica. He went to primary school at (INAUDIBLE) and (INAUDIBLE), gymnasium and the Faculty of Philosophy in Novi Sad. He is one of the protagonists and collaborators of Novi Sad (INAUDIBLE) in 1986 to 1990. He is the ideological creator of the National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and is the responsible editor of the gazette Srpska (INAUDIBLE) of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem in 1991. He lives in Novi Sad and works in an enterprise as an employee."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to call your attention to page 175 of the book. There is a copy of a document under the number 2. I have had prepared a copy of this document along with an English translation -- I will mark this as Prosecutor's exhibit 197 for the original Serb version and Prosecutor's exhibit 197A as the English translation. (Handed). I would ask you, if you could, to read out the introductory paragraph of this document, which appears on the first page, directly under the number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, do you mean this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, directly under the number 2, the Serb version. Perhaps it would be helpful for him to have the book to read from. It may be clearer than reading from the copies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can read it out. If this relates to the text: "The HDZ sells weapons to the Croats and the Serbs." Do you have that text in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe it is directly under the number 2, at the bottom of the page there is a number 2, and then directly under that there is a statement. I know the 2 is a little difficult to see, because it was highlighted. Again, perhaps it would be helpful if the witness had the book from which to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "To all the information media in Yugoslavia: Representatives of the Serb people in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem elected today the Serb National Council for this part of the present Republic of Croatia. For the Secretary-General of the Serb National Society, which will in the future represent the interests of the Serb people, who have lived in this region for centuries, Ilija Kovacevic was elected, a prominent fighter for Serb national rights. He is a Serb from Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milinkovic, if you could go to the following page, and under the caption "The Serb National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem" there are numbered paragraphs. If you can read paragraphs 1, 2 and 3, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "1. Does not accept the solution whereby, the present republics of Croatia and Slovenia without the consent of the Serb people of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem are withdrawing their territories from the State of Yugoslavia. "2. As the only legitimate organ of the Serb people of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, it will represent the interests of these people in all negotiations on the future of Yugoslavia and the future of the Serb people in the present Republic of Croatia. "3. It orders all Serbs holding any position or public office at any level from the local communes to the republic and federation, except those in the Croat SABOR Parliament, to remain in office and consistently in all those positions, represent the interests of the Serb people. "4. Calls on its Croat brothers to fulfil the most sacred of all human duties and bring all their extremists imbued with anti-Serb sentiment to a recognition of rights, recalling that all the wars fought so far are over and hoping that, in this way, an end will be put to the several centuries of genocide against Serbs in Croatia and to the irrational hatred of the Croat national fighters, for everything Serb. Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem have been Serb land since ancient times and the members of the other peoples whose fate it was to live alongside the Serbs in this land are requested and expected not to do to the Serb people anything that they would not want the Serbs to do to them. The Serb national entity is permanently rooted in these regions, in the same way that the Serb soul is indestructible. It is not good that pressures, overt or covert, auger Serb casualties, nor does the Serb people in Croatia need to build upon such victims a new Kosovo temple of its rebirth -- Christmas 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This would be referring to the Orthodox Christmas, would it not, which is in January 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably -- if it is 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, I would call your attention to page 179 of the book, and direct your attention to the document which appears under the number 5. When is this document dated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this relates to item 5, 3 February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have had prepared a copy of this document, again along with an English translation. I will mark them as Prosecutor's exhibit 198 for the original Serb version and Prosecutor's exhibit 198A for the English translation. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not understand -- do you wish me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, I would like copies to go to the court, first. Now I would ask you, if you would, to read out where it starts "The Serb National Council Regional Board for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem proposes" and there are several numbered paragraphs, if you could read all these paragraphs, please, starting with number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "1. That all contested and uncontested regions in the territory of the present Republic of Croatia be defined. "1.1.
