The uncontested regions are those where Croat statehood was established back in the Middle Ages and where the Serb population has never constituted a majority. "1.2. The contested regions, at this time, are those regions which have been inhabited by the Serb population since ancient times and over which, as a result of the military power of the Austrian empire, the authority of the Croat SABOR Parliament occasionally and gradually extended, so that, today, with the help of the AVNOJ principles, the Republic of Croatia has been established as the successor State of the independent State of Croatia. According to this view, in addition to Kninska Krajina and the Serb municipalities in Lika, Banja, and Kordun as well as other possible territories relevant to the delineation of borders, the contested territories include Baranja, Western Srem, (from the Ilok-Lovas-Jamena line to the Cepin-Trnjani line) and Slavonia from Cepin-Trnjani line and to the Ilova river and a point 10 kilometres west of Virovitica. "2. The legal system of the present Republic of Croatia and the authority of the Croat SABOR are to be suspended in all the contested regions and they should be placed instead under the direct jurisdiction of the presidency of the SFRY and the federal SUP. This jurisdiction would be in effect until precise criteria for the delineation of borders between the Serb and Croat peoples are determined, including the voluntary relocation of all interested Serbs, Croats and members of the different national minorities inhabiting these regions, across the line which would be established as the future border between the Croat nation State and Yugoslavia. Any other interested citizens currently residing east or west of the border of the contested territories as outlined here may avail themselves of the right to voluntary relocation."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn to page 183, where there is a copy of a document under the number 10. Again, I have prepared a copy of this document which I will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 199. I must apologise, however, since this is a somewhat lengthier document, the English translation has not yet been completed, but, as soon as it is, I will supplement the record with that document and we will mark it as Prosecutor's exhibit 199A. That should be later today or Monday, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would just ask you to read out from the top of the page on the second page, I believe, through paragraph 5, the second page, I think, if you can turn the page, and there are some numbers, if you can read from the beginning and the numbered paragraphs 1 through 5 and then paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 1: "The Serb people in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem is an indivisible part of the sovereign Serb people living in Yugoslavia. Therefore, the territory which it populates, they enjoy the sovereign rights of the Serb people. "2. The realisation of the sovereign rights of the Serb people in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem is expressed in sovereign autonomy, which understands the supreme legislative, executive and legal powers in autonomy. It is the matter of autonomy in the sense of this declaration -- this includes language, the upbringing of children and the youth, education, religion, health protection, the protection of the environment, nature and cultural monuments, the creation, that is, that the national heritage be protected, protection of law and order, as well as other things directly connected to these which are determined by the Statute on autonomy, or by an autonomous decree. "4. In order to implement sovereign autonomy of the Serb people in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, the Statute on autonomy establishes its organs and organisations. It is the rights of the organs of autonomy to prescribe and collect taxes necessary to perform its activities in all matters of autonomy and that, via its organisations and enterprises, deal with corresponding necessary economic activities. "5. In keeping with the Statute governing autonomy, the organs of autonomy shall cooperate with other parts of the Serb people in Yugoslavia, its representatives, its political and other organisations and institutions, and, in that sense, can, in matters of autonomy, conclude separate agreements."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you would go to paragraph 10, please, and just read that, and the date that this was adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Sovereign Serb autonomy of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem exists and acts within the frameworks of the President Republic of Croatia only on condition that Yugoslavia exists as a Federal State. If a Yugoslavia of this kind ceases to exist, or it becomes transformed into a conglomeration of independent States, this autonomy will continue to exist as part of the matrix State of the Serb people." The date of Simun Mirotocivi, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know what that date is, I believe that is a Saint's day, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- maybe it is -- I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And the matrix State of the Serb people is Serbia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs in Croatia considered it to be Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this point, I would ask you to turn to page 194 and direct your attention to the document which appears under the number 23, and if you can, say what the date is of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 23 -- there is no date there under number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: There is not a date --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is, up on the top -- it is 26 February 1991 -- in Osijek, 26 February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a copy of this document in Serb and English. I will mark the Serb version as Prosecutor's exhibit 200 and the English version as Prosecutor's exhibit 200A. (Handed). I would ask you to read out this document in its entirety, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Proceeding from the declaration on sovereign autonomy of the Serb people of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem in Osijek adopted on 26 February 1991, the Serb National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, at its session held on the holiday of Cvijeta on 31 March 1991, adopts a decision to annex Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, excluding areas which are part of the Serb autonomous district of Krajina to the autonomous province of Vojvodina, namely the Republic of Serbia. The council requests of the President of the Assembly of the autonomous province of Vojvodina and the National Assembly of Serbia to call early sessions of the assemblies to make the following decisions: to join Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem to the autonomous province of Voyvodina, namely the Republic of Serbia, and to establish temporary organs of executive and judicial authority in the conjoined areas. For the Serb National Council, Ilija Petrovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Finally, I would ask you to turn to the end of the book, immediately after page 163, and to examine the map that appears on that page, and at this time, I would distribute copies of this, which is marked as Prosecutor's exhibit 201. (Handed). Looking at this map, it encompasses a region which includes the municipalities of Osijek and Vinkovski, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the municipality of Vinkovski, as far as I can see -- the municipality of Vukovar, and I am not sure how big the area of the municipality of Vinkovski is, so I do not know if it is the whole area or part of it. I think that it was not the whole of the area of Osijek, and the municipality of Vukovar in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask that the witness be shown defence exhibit 19, please, and 19A being the English translation. Do you have this in front of you now, Mr. Milinkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you could look at the various regions, which are indicated as being part of this Serb district, which appear under article 11, it indicates the registered municipal land areas of number 1; Vukovar, number 2; Beli Manastir, number 3; Vinkovski, number 4; Dalj and number 5; Osijek, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Under the section for Osijek, it includes the city of Osijek, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "Osijek" in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, under the section for Vinkovski, number 3, that listing, it also includes the city of Vinkovski, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Osijek, after point 5, it says "Osijek, temporary seat in tenure".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It has a number of municipalities, which includes the number of towns or cities, which also includes the city of Osijek, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And under the provision for Vinkovski, paragraph 3, it also includes the city of Vinkovski, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says Vinkovski -- it says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you happen to know if Osijek and Vinkovski have a majority Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Vinkovski, there was a relatively small percentage of Serb population in the town itself -- in Osijek, perhaps it was one quarter of the population, but I am not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But, it would be fair to say that there was a substantial majority of Croats in both those areas, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, going back through all these documents that you looked at in the book, all of these items were dated on or before 31 March 1991, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the date for this last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: With the exception of this last one, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I imagine it is so -- this is December 1991, the last one, if I am not mistaken, that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct. The other documents that you read from the book, however, all dated; the first one from January 1991, then 3 February 1991, 26 February 1991, and the last one, 31 March 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So all of those pronouncements by this Serb National Council, which says that it is the legitimate voice of the Serb people, were enacted prior to the events at Plitvice, or at the latest on the same day at Plitvice; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them obviously before that, but some of these documents also came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If Plitvice occurred on 31 March and the last of those documents was dated that date, then they all occurred prior to, or on the same date, as Plitvice; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that a declaration to the effect that a region of Croat territory was being annexed to the Republic of Serbia is a provocation to the Croat authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, in the same way this is a provocation as the proclamation of independence within Yugoslavia is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But that occurred three months after that, did it not, on 25 June 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, but, after Croatia had separated itself from Yugoslavia -- the proclamation of independence from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you understand why the Croat authorities might seek to remove from office someone who has joined an organisation that declares a region of Croatia belongs to another State, declares that Croat law does not apply and advocates a relocation of populations across redrawn borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have Mr. Dokmanovic in mind, I never heard him state anything of that nature. He has not told me that personally, and he has never said anything of that sort in public, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. I would tender all of these exhibits. This would be 194 through, I believe, to 201. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If the book is admitted into evidence, can we have it submitted in its entirety? I will ask the witness to read from page 40 of that book. Could you please read from page 40 -- if the defence has no objections? Article 64 of this book -- it is not fair to make partial presentations before the court. It is fair to show the book itself. In this book, it says that Slavko Dokmanovic is not a member of the Serb National Council. Could you please read page 64, this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We certainly have no objection to him reading it and no-one has attempted to stop him from putting in anything else. There was one additional exhibit that I wished to present in conjunction with this. There is a summary in English of the Serb National Council, which I have also copied. I would offer that as exhibit 202, which gives an overall summary of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is a summary by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: By the author -- it appears in the book itself. It is in English. I would present that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The whole book is an exhibit, and has been tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well then. It is up to your Honours, if you would like this or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we do. I was just asking, in addition to the various parts, whether the whole book has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 196 is the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read from page 40, this is Prosecutor's exhibit 196, footnote 64, if I am not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to read slowly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: : "Slavko Dokmanovic, Trpinja, 1949, an engineer of agriculture until the war for the independence of Krajina, he was President of the municipality of Vukovar. It is mostly thanks to his inability that the Assembly of the Municipality of Vukovar, although having a Serb majority, allowed the Secretariat of the Interior in Vukovar to be dissolved, which allowed the Ustasha police headquarters in Vinkovski to take care of the Serb population. In the Serb National Council of Knin, he was a member, but he withdrew from there. In the Government of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, he was Minister of Agriculture. He is the director of the renewed Vukovar Vinarija within the agricultural combine. Since the end of June 1994, he has again become President of the Municipality of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the legitimacy of the Serb National Council? Was this a body that was elected at certain elections, which was a representative body, which represents the population of that territory or not. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the body of the Serb National Council was established in Knin somewhat earlier and, as far as I can recollect, that is why Mr. Dokmanovic's resignation was asked for by the HDZ, and, to the best of my knowledge, it was supposed to protect the interests of the Serb population in Croatia -- only protect their interests. It had no other significance as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, they were not chosen at elections and it does not legitimately represent the Serb will in Croatia anyway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure whether or not there were any elections; I just know that it was supposed to protect the imperilled interests of the Serb people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who comprised this Serb National Council? Are you sure about this and, if you are so sure, how do you know that Slavko Dokmanovic was a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no opportunity of seeing any proof demonstrating that Slavko Dokmanovic was a member of the Serb National Council in Knin. I just remember that the deputies of the HDZ in the Municipal Assembly were saying so, and that is why they asked for a vote of confidence for Slavko Dokmanovic, but as far as Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem, I did not speak about this at all in my statement and, as far as I can remember, Mr. Dokmanovic did not really take part in this at all, because what was mentioned a few minutes ago was a different Serb National Council and that is the Serb National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You read a few minutes ago the declaration of the will of the people of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranje and Zapadni Srem at the request of the Prosecutor and this was Prosecutor's exhibit 199 in its Serb version. Could the witness be shown this document once again? In the footnote it says: "who signed this declaration?". Do you know who signed this declaration, so this is page 185, footnote 16 of the Serb version -- do you know who signed this? What we are primarily interested in is whether you know that Slavko Dokmanovic signed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is page 185, and there is a footnote, number 16 down there, which is linked to the text of the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The declaration was signed by 16 [sic] persons, 10 from the founding meeting and seven new ones. I do not know who signed this, but, to the best of my knowledge, Mr. Dokmanovic was not a member of that National Council -- all the documents that were presented by the Prosecutor pertained exclusively to the National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there were two National Councils?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were two National Councils, and the author of this book, on page 40, mentions specifically that Mr. Dokmanovic was not a member of that National Council, but that he joined the National Council of Knin. It was established somewhat earlier and not a single piece of evidence is related to that National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that. I think he has mis-characterised it unless there was a mis-translation earlier. I do not think there was a statement that he did not belong to the council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. What it said was that he was a member of the council in Knin. I would ask that the witness reread that section, or at least point out exactly where it states that he was not a member of the council for Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem, as he has just asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please read again the relevant section?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Page 40, footnote 64?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again: "Slavko Dokmanovic, Trpinja 1949, engineer of agriculture. Until the war for the independence of Krajina, he was President of the Vukovar municipality. It is mostly thanks to his inability that the Assembly of the Municipality of Vukovar, although enjoying a Serb majority population, allowed the Secretariat of the Interior to be dissolved in Vukovar. In this way, the Ustasha Croat police from Vinkovski was allowed to take care of the Serb population in Vukovar. In the Serb National Council of Knin he was a member but he withdrew from there. In the Government of Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem, he was Minister of Agriculture . He is a director of Vukovar Vinarija which was renewed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, can we thus conclude that this footnote is actually a CV of Slavko Dokmanovic, because obviously, that is how he was first mentioned in this book -- this is a CV of Slavko Dokmanovic, that is, that if he were a member of another National Council, obviously this would have been mentioned; they would not have only referred to as the Serb National Council in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, because this is a footnote provided by the author of this book, because, had Mr. Dokmanovic been a member of the National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem, this certainly would have been highlighted in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any other document which would link Slavko Dokmanovic with the National Council of Slavonia, Baranje and Zapadni Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that I am not aware of any document of this kind, and I am sure that Mr. Dokmanovic never even mentioned to me, on any occasion, the Serb National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem because to the best of my knowledge, in that period, he no longer enjoyed any confidence among the Serbs of that part of Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem. In that period, he lost all credibility among all the Serbs, just as I lost it, and many others who advocated a different cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why? What happened; could you tell me why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were advocating a peaceful solution, to resolve the conflict by peaceful means, not by an armed conflict and because we were accused, Mr. Dokmanovic, I, and other people, of insufficiently being engaged in the protection of the rights and interests of Serbs in that part of Slavonia, Baranja and Zapadni Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Boro Savic -- we are going back to a different subject -- Mr. Borov Savic in connection to the incident in Plitvice. Who is Mr. Boro Savic and where is he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borov Savic lived in Vukovar, and I think he still lives in Vukovar. I got to know him better only after he returned from Plitvice upon his arrest, and he told me that he and Hadzic were coming back from Knin from some kind of meeting, that they were staying at the hotel in Plitvice and that during the night, there was shooting and they were arrested there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I also wish to go back to the question of Borovo Selo -- the persons who obstructed the passage of the military column that tried to get in, they were also armed. Were these official formations, was this the police, or were these armed civilians who were preventing the army from passing through -- who are these armed civilians, where were they, and tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2 May, when, from the office of Mr. Dokmanovic, I took the official car of the President of the Municipality and Mr. Modalek was in the car with me and I went to see why the army was not coming to separate these people, and I got to the exit out of Vukovar towards Osijek where the tanks were lined up and several hundred civilians -- there were children there, too, so they were all there -- some of them were armed and were wearing uniforms, but also there were some people who were wearing civilian clothes and who had weapons, and I think that these could not have been regular forces of the police, but these had to be armed civilians -- probably paramilitary formations of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I wanted to know about the author of the book -- is he alive?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I do not know, your Honour. I have no information on this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I help you? He will be one of the witnesses on the video link -- no, he is alive and lives in Novi Sad -- Koncarevic will be on the video link -- I mixed that up. He is alive, yes. The videotape, your Honours, that I gave as supporting material -- let me remind you -- one of the witnesses in the indictment said that Slavko Dokmanovic was criticised for being on television in Novi Sad. I think Mr. Williamson will recall this -- for having taken part in a television programme in Novi Sad. I have the tape, I will let you look at it and that is the Ilija Petrovic in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions. You insisted on a particular point, even a few minutes ago, namely that both you and Mr. Dokmanovic were moderates, among the Serbs. You just spoke of loss of credibility among the Serbs, because of your peaceful attitude. At one point, according to you, both you and Mr. Dokmanovic were regarded as traitors by some Serbs, I imagine extremists. We saw a document where mention is made of a CV, Mr. Dokmanovic's CV, of his inability in the Assembly, which means that it is a document which is rather critical of Mr. Dokmanovic. However, how do you explain that around probably July, August -- I do not know the exact date -- Mr. Dokmanovic, in spite of this loss of credibility, became a Minister of Agriculture of the Government of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja and Srem -- he became an authority of a Government controlling that particular area of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the circumstances. Let me repeat that I was in Vukovar only until the end of July. I did not go to Vukovar after that date, so that I do not know the circumstances under which this happened, but I think it was considerably later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I would imagine that the Government presided over by Goran Hadzic would not have appointed a traitor as a member of this particular Government, so you do not know any explanation of how to reconcile two seemingly contradictory facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was not present in Vukovar, I was not in contact with the people -- I was near Belgrade where I live today and perform my duties -- so that I have no information which would be relevant, that is to say, on the basis of which Mr. Dokmanovic was included in the Government, but I am sure that, in the period when I was there, both he and I had a lot of unpleasantness from the Serbs there, who called us quite publicly "traitors".

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a few minutes ago some uniformed civilians who, according to you, were members of the HDZ, and you also previously had mentioned those uniformed civilians when you were talking of that episode of the Combi where you found yourself in a particular situation. Could you give us a description of these uniformed civilians. Were they wearing military uniforms? What sort of uniforms were they wearing -- were they wearing insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of them had some camouflage uniforms, very often incomplete, only parts of uniforms but, as a rule, they were, as I say, just parts of uniforms. They were either camouflage uniforms and often weapons were seen in the hands of people who were in civilian clothing and were together with these partially uniformed individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But you inferred from their wearing some sort of camouflage uniform, the fact that they were members of paramilitary units -- of Croat paramilitary units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, because, in addition to the members of the Croat police forces wearing regular uniforms on the barricades and particularly in the case of Borovo Selo, there were individuals, a significant number of individuals, with long weaponry, wearing partial uniforms, usually camouflage uniforms, and a lot of people were in civilian clothing, but they were together, with the Police Forces of Croatia, on the basis of which I concluded that it was a question of paramilitary formations. Otherwise, when Mr. Mercep took over the National defence, was in fact in command -- I personally saw that, even before that, that is to say, before 2 May, Mr. Sredoselac who was the commander of the police station at Vukovar, was criticised as being just a youth in his police station, whereas formation-wise, Mr. Mercep should have had no links at all with the police, because he was head of a political Party. On the basis of this, I gained the impression that in fact it was he who commanded the police station and not Mr. Sredoselac, the official commander. I had occasion to convince myself of this on several occasions and Mr. Sredoselac acknowledged he was not in control of his men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now we are talking of the Croats. The normal perception of a person, particularly a political leader, or somebody involved in politics or in the public administration, the normal perception, to see him wearing a uniform -- a military uniform, a camouflage uniform, would give rise to the assumption, to the man in the street, as it were, that he was a member of a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well I knew the uniforms of the regular police force of Croatia. I was acquainted with those uniforms, and all the people who were with them at the barricades or at positions of this kind, usually barricades, that I passed through wearing other uniforms or civilians with long weaponry could only be treated in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: One last and very minor question: you said yesterday that before May you had the opportunity to go to Trpinja by car and fetch Mr. Dokmanovic, to take him to Vukovar, because of the possibility or fear of incidents and so on. I understand this happened quite a few times and this was intended to protect Mr. Dokmanovic. How far is Trpinja from Vukovar in terms of kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So normally, how long would it take you to go by car from Trpinja to Vukovar, as a rule of thumb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions? There is no objection to the witness being released? Thank you so much, Mr. Milinkovic, for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think we can start with our next witness. I am happy to see that Mr. Fila and I have a special way of communicating by gestures. We come from the same area of the Mediterranean, you are of Greek origin, I think?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is a very quick way of communicating -- but not improper, because it is in open court, so everybody can watch us. I hope we can finish by 1.15 with both witnesses, assuming the Prosecutor does not have too many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I fear not. We shall try of course, but I fear that we will not succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It goes without saying that we do not intend to compress or curtail the rights of the defence. This would be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We do not expect long testimonies from these witnesses, but after all we do only half an hour and a half at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was raising this issue, because in reading yesterday the written statements of the two witnesses, I realised that they are very short, so I was wondering whether the oral testimony could be short as well. Good morning Mr. Vracaric, may I ask you to make the sworn declaration? ZDRAVKO VRACARIC:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Examination-in-chief by MR. PETROVIC.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vracaric, did you, on 11 September 1997, talk to lawyer Ore, the investigating individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in Vukovar, and made a statement to what he asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at the document and tell us whether that is the statement that you gave to Mr. Oro? (Handed). The statement by Mr. Vracaric, in Serb, I tender as D30 and D30A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my statement and that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born, what are you by profession and your place of employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Trpinja on 29 March 1948. That is where I lived until the third grade primary school and then I went to Vukovar, all my antecedents were born in Trpinja. I moved to Vukovar where I completed gymnasium and later I went to the Faculty of Political Science, the group for sociology, and I am by profession a Professor of Sociology. My last employment was in a private enterprise for the training of drivers. It was called the (INAUDIBLE) Test, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are from the same village. I have known Slavko personally. Our families knew each personally. I am one year older than Mr. Dokmanovic. We went to the same primary school. Later on, we went to the same secondary school. As I interrupted my studies for one year, we were in the same form in the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1968, in the final year of gymnasium, I became a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and I was a member of the League until the dissolution of the League of Communists. After that, I was not a member of any political Party. However, when the multi-party system in the Republic of Croatia started up, I found myself, as an option, in the SDP Party, but I was never a member of the Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hold a membership card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I never had a membership card and, like most of the Serbs, the large majority, like Mr. Dokmanovic as well, we never had a membership card.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the first multi-Party elections for the Municipal Assembly for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did and I found myself to be on the list for the Associated Labour Council Chamber, and all the citizens of Vukovar who knew me and knew the nature of the work I did as the owner of a driving school, I was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you have contact for the first time with the Croat Democratic Union or any of its members, or attended one of its meetings and your impressions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the part of Vukovar which was called Mitnica, and that was the local community called Vladimir Nazor. Quite by chance, I had my first concrete meeting with the HDZ there, that is to say, my colleague, Gordana Gojic, she was in the same local community -- we were both activists there -- informed me one day that there would be a meeting of some kind without any invitations, and that none of the Serbs had been invited to the meeting, and it would be a good idea, she said, to go and see what it was going to be about, because allegedly the HDZ would be having a founding meeting for the Vladimir Nazor local community and that is what happened. We went to the hall, there were quite a lot of people there, we came on time, we took our places and three of us there were there Gordana Gojic, myself, and a retired worker of the SUP at the time, Mr. Zezey -- I forget his first name. The hall was filled by our neighbours -- all of them were well-known to us. There were lots of people who had never been active in manifestations of this kind before. Then, a team of individuals arrived, some 15 of them, perhaps a little more, they entered the hall, when the hall was already full. Mr. Tomislav Mercep was among them, Mr. Gazo was there, Sabljic and others. Some people said there were a lot of people from Vinkovski and Osijek. They were allegedly activists of the HDZ. Mr. Seremet, I believe, chaired the meeting -- I do not know his first name, but he is also from our local community. Mr. Mercep on the occasion held a fiery speech -- fairly well prepared, I would say -- and that was the first time I actually saw Mr. Tomislav Mercep, although I knew his brother, Simun, from earlier on. I knew him as a huntsman and as a dog lover, and the speech held by Mr. Mercep was a political speech -- a political campaign -- membership in the HDZ, what the Croats should do, their tasks, how to make the organisation a more massive organisation, that this was the one true Party for the first time where a Croat could find himself, and what I always recall, and which worried me a little on the occasion was something he said -- he said a sentence to the following effect: "Finally, there will be a redistribution of property. The Serbs will no longer enjoy the large houses and property they own now -- there will be a redistribution of work posts. Croats will not be citizens of the second order any more. Of course, there are places for the Serbs, too, for those who remain. There are enough shovels for those who remain and there will be enough work for everybody" and there was an applause after that, and then they moved towards electing the activists who the organising born, Mr. Anto Beljo became a member, Colak, my neighbour, Daljic, Istuk Seremet himself and many others, I do not recall exactly who. Somebody happened to mention on the occasion that there were those sitting there who should not be there -- they probably had us in mind. But we were told that it did not matter that we were there, and that we would be able to leave the meeting quite safely. That is what happened. In the evening hours, the three of us safely left the meeting. That was my first contact with the HDZ and it was in March -- mid March I should say -- I think I was almost certain that it was 12 March 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, how did the first multi-party elections for the Croat SABOR --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I followed the elections in Vukovar, that is to say, the local elections, but the mass media wrote about this and spoke about this and I was able to see the elections there. We hoped that the situation would be more favourable for the SDP but, quite obviously, through the electoral system and the other available media, we know what happened -- in the Republic of Croatia, the HDZ was victorious, whereas in Vukovar, the situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the pre-election campaign like in Vukovar and the situation in the town in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was very lively. Two parties were present on the political scene -- the HDZ as an exclusively National Party full of burgeoning efforts and exclusive nature -- all their meetings were very loud with a lot of flags, a lot of various insignias, the checker board, the Croat insignia, and they were mass meetings, and many people were present. You could see that there were a lot of financial resources invested, that the media paid a great deal of attention -- there were a lot of slogans, posters and so on and so forth, and Vukovar was well covered. On the other hand, the SDP based its campaign on the fact that it was not a nationalistic Party, that there was enough room for everybody in the Party and it advocated something that we found favourable as Serbs, that is cohabitation -- not brotherhood and unity perhaps, but cohabitation, that we could live alongside each other, work alongside each other peacefully and that there was room for everybody in the Party. I was in Vukovar at one promotion meeting for the -- in the centre of town, which rallied a lot of people and just like all our meetings of that kind, it evolved peacefully. As I say, these were two opposites. Perhaps it was interesting to see those opposites at the time, but it did herald a complex and difficult situation, which was to ensue, because the meetings of this kind, from the HDZ meetings of this kind, one could always feel endeavours to ensure a better morrow only for the members of one nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the conclusion of the elections for the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar at those first multi-Party elections and at a local level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They finished as we foresaw, that is to say, the SDP won. Two-thirds or more of the members of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar were from the SDP's list; the HDZ, led my Mercep, won, in our assessment, a maximum of the votes that they could have won under those circumstances -- it is quite obvious that they were not very satisfied, but that was the outcome of the elections. With the number of votes we gained, we were satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar constituted after the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality was constituted according to the Rules of Procedure and just as other assemblies were constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You were elected a Deputy of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the Chamber of Associated Labour. The Assembly was constituted and we immediately took up our seats -- the HDZ was to the left of us and we, as the vast majority, were on the other side. Immediately after the beginning, one could see that the HDZ wished to obstruct the meeting -- they reacted very loudly and always under Mr. Mercep's command. If Mr. Mercep got up and asked people to leave the hall, the others got up, too. If he said that they should remain, they remained. But, nonetheless, we succeeded in harmonising our views as to basic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was elected President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two candidates for the President of the Assembly. I did not actually take part in the consultations -- inter-Party negotiations -- like most of the deputies I was faced with an alternative -- either Slavko Dokmanovic or Ms. Bojana Peter. It was quite normal that all of us from the SDP, and especially all the Serbs, to vote for Slavko Dokmanovic for the following reasons: first of all, Mr. Dokmanovic was a highly educated individual. He was a prosperous individual. He was a stable personality, a man with broad views, and a very moderate option, which corresponded to our needs, which suited us. He was a moderate, as I say -- always in favour of cohabitation, of the fact that we should all stay in the area, and somebody who wanted everybody to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar at the time, the first problems arose between the Croats and the Serbs with regard to nationality. What did the Deputy President of the Municipal Assembly try to do to overcome tensions as far as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although we had the vast majority in the Municipal Assembly, and percentage-wise the HDZ as a Party had a fewer seats in the bodies, commissions and so on, Slavko Dokmanovic insisted that we try and dovetail this with the HDZ members, and that we should agree to give them more seats, so that the climate of work and tolerance would prevail and that is what happened. They got more seats than they would objectively merit according to the percentages. Mr. Matovic was elected deputy -- Vice-President -- they were given seats in the commissions, and everything was done to work on the basis of a dialogue. Mr. Dokmanovic advocated that, but so did I as well as Mr. Maksim Vojnovic and others. We tried to do everything in our power to condemn excess situations. There was understanding on both sides, Marin Vidic Bili was very tolerant, for example. He was along the same lines as we were ourselves very often. When I talked to many of the HDZ deputies at the beginning, they also condemned individual excessive conduct, but the next day this excessive conduct would continue, so it is one thing what was being said and another thing what was being done. Slavko Dokmanovic, at the clubs of deputies of the SDP, always advocated one and the same thing -- let us seek compromise, let us be tolerant, let us be patient, do not answer provocations, do not let ourselves, as the majority Party, be responsible for any serious incident. Those were always the suggestions he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Tomislav Mercep on several occasions. Can you tell us something about his role in Vukovar in that period in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from seeing him for the first time in the local community of Vladimir Nazor, we got to know each other better when we began working in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. It so happened that the offices of my enterprise and the offices of the HDZ, Mercep's Party, were right next to one another -- we were only separated by a wall. That is how we saw each other work -- outside the Assembly. Very often, Mr. Mercep would come to see me. I always had good whiskey to offer him, because after all, that is the kind of job I had -- we were supposed to be good hosts to all our clients, and I would also come to see him and he respected me for at least three reasons, I believe; first of all, I was a personal friend for several years of Mr. Slavko Degoricija, who already, at that stage, was Assistant Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. Secondly, Mercep's wife attended this driving school that I worked in, and under certain privileged conditions so to speak -- she did not have to wait in line, she could choose the driving instructor she wanted, et cetera. It was only natural -- we were neighbours, you know. Thirdly, he respected me as a business person, because I had a very successful enterprise, and, when journalists would come to see him -- different kinds of journalists, he would introduce me as a Serb who is successful and who is not hindered in any way in his business. Very soon, Mercep became popular among the members of the HDZ. He had an exceptional energy -- physically and mentally he was quite fit and also he was very ambitious. From morning until night, people came to his office and went out of it and, as I said, his office was right next door to mine. Knowing the setting there, these were people who were really anonymous, who were on the margins of social life there, but that is where he felt fine -- he was popular among them. He was liked by them and it became obvious that it was not only that he held the baton of a conductor in the Assembly but, as time went by, he held the baton of a conductor over other structures, too -- in the police, in the civilian life, he was at the centre of everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mind if we now have a recess? I would propose only 10 minutes -- is that alright? I hope the interpreters do not mind -- you do mind -- 15 minutes then. (11.55 a.m.). (A short break). (12.10).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: At 1.30 we have a meeting with the President and the other presiding judges of the various Chambers to agree upon a court schedule for the next few months. This also relates to our trial. I wonder whether we could be as expeditious as possible, in particular, the witness could give us short answers. Let us make an effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We shall certainly try to make the questions as concise as possible and to make the witness's answers as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, very briefly, I wish to recall an interesting episode with Slavko Degoricija, your personal acquaintance with him, and is there anything interesting to mention in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said already --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But please be brief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that we had been friends for a long time. Slavko Dokmanovic knew from me that I was friends with Mr. Degoricija. At one point in time he said, "Why don't you ask your friend to come and go hunting with us here in Trpinja, so that he can see what kind of people we are like, so we could socialise a bit." I told Mr. Degoricija about this and, although he was a passionate huntsman, he could not make it, because he had a very busy schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the armament of the members of the HDZ in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how, when, and in what way, people were armed, but in the early spring, some time around 5 o'clock in the afternoon, I came to my offices, because a new driving course was supposed to begin. I saw quite a few people in front of the office of the HDZ. I went to see Mercep before this was to begin. I entered the door. The room was full. I was surprised. On the right-hand side by the wall there were a few civilians -- they were sitting on the floor, actually -- and they had automatic rifles, and those small green-grey bags. I was really surprised. Until then, I had never seen armed persons in the offices of the HDZ. The next day I saw Mr. Mercep and I said, "What was all that about? What do you need all this for, Mercep?" He said, "Don't be surprised by this. That's the way it is. Is somebody bothering you; is somebody threatening you? Has somebody done anything to you?" I said "no", he said, "Mind your own business. We are going to attain our objectives and we believe all is fair in that respect and even Croats who oppose us will be removed", and I did not comment on that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, do you know any specific cases of pressure against Serbs who lived in Vukovar -- was there any destruction of their property; were they expelled from work; did they have to move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go into individual specific cases, because, as each day went by, something new happened. It was even unusual if nothing happened. People started moving out en masse, particularly after Borovo Selo. I know only one specific case because it is a friend of mine who was concerned in it -- he is deceased now -- it is Mr. Jovo Jakoljevic his nickname was Rakijica -- he was a passionate huntsman like me. I would often come to see him. He was running a state-owned shop of hunting arms and, in 1991, I stopped by his shop to see him and he complained to me that Mercep and his people were threatening him, and that he was supposed to hand over these hunting arms to them, especially carbines, but he said he would not do it. I said, "Jovan, aren't you frightened?. It's your life that's at stake. Why don't you give it to them?". He said, "No, I don't really want to do that. I'm going to give it to the military barracks." I think some time in June, Jovan was tragically killed. I do not know specifically how he was killed or who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was this last meeting of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly scheduled for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until April all of this went by some how, but then in May, I think around 17 May, a meeting was scheduled. We came in front of the Assembly. There was a biggish group there already of members and supporters of the HDZ and they did not let us go into the Assembly building. It is interesting that, from the first time it was constituted, there was always some kind of a pressure group there -- 10, 20 to 30 people -- they were always in front of the Assembly. They were not members of the Assembly, but they were there, either by accident or at someone's invitation -- they were this unpleasant pressure group outside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that that day, when this last attempt was made to have a meeting of the Municipal Assembly held -- was that the last day when this Assembly actually functioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I never even received an invitation for an Assembly meeting, and the Assembly was not functioning to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until when did Mr. Dokmanovic perform the duties of President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already after the events of May in Borovo Selo, his position was seriously shaken and with a great degree of caution, he would come from time to time to the best of my recollection, Mr. Milinkovic would bring him in and after that he could not really come to the municipality any more. He would often complain to me and to Mr. Maksim Vojnovic. We would sit there together at the SDK. He would complain he was receiving threats and he would say his life was in danger. We said, come on man, do not come, because your life is more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was the Assembly of the municipality of Vukovar dissolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, at the beginning of July, a decree was issued by the Government and the Assembly was dissolved. Although I never received an official document saying so, it was a load off my chest that this had happened, because Mr. Vojnovic told me on the phone that the Assembly was no longer in existence, so it suited me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Vukovar and on what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Vukovar on 31 August 1991. I was taken out of Vukovar by a Croat, Ivan Matic, who was best man at my wedding. He had a former pupil, who was a member of the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, and his pupil took me, my wife, and the wife of my best man, and a certain Dorde, who was a butcher -- he took us out of Vukovar and we passed by many ZNG posts, but really no-one stopped us and this ZNG, this friend of my best friend -- I think his last name was Milas-- mill as, he took us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you mentioned that you knew in person Marin Vidic Bili. Could the witness please be shown D8, exhibit D8 -- could you please look at this document and could you please say what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know this document. I have it at home until the present day. The document was given to me by Mr. Marin Vidic Bili -- perhaps a day or two after this document -- after this date which is on the document, he came to my home, he, my wife and I sat on the terrace and we had some ice-cream and we discussed the situation. Bili was always the representative of a moderate option and we had a lot in common. We became friends when the Assembly was constituted, and I even as a personal favour to him, organised a driver's course in Lovas, in his native town. He came to see me that day and he complained about everything that was happening in Vukovar. He also noticed that a lot of Serbs were moving out of Vukovar, Serbs were moving out in all sorts of ways -- some of them bribed HDZ people, some took advantage of their friendships, but everyone tried to escape as best they could. He told me then, Bili told me then, that certain extremist groups got out of control, that everyone was doing what he wanted to do and that he was afraid that he would be held accountable, because of that, as the representative, and he said, "This is my last attempt" and he gave me this document "to prevent the chaos that may ensue if this is not stopped." He said "Zdravko, tell the Serbs not to move out, tell the Serbs you know not to move out. I am giving this to you, you are a prominent person. Show this to them," although he personally did not believe that anything would improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Slavko Dokmanovic was in Vukovar during war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic did not stay in Vukovar during the war operations, just as I was not in Vukovar during the war operations. May I just say the following? After the Borovo events, Slavko was labelled a traitor. He was accused of having informed the army that came in and saved the members of the MUP. He was also accused of having handed over Vukovar to the HDZ, an extremist HDZ. He knew that messages were coming in from so-called headquarters all over Vukovar -- various villages, Negoslavci, even all the way to Sid. It was said he did not dare come back to Vukovar and he should not dare come back to Vukovar. He came to see me in Ilok -- on 14 November 1991, I started working as the director of Agrokomerc in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may I show you a document at this point -- could I ask you kindly to show the witness this document? (Handed). It is dated 13 November 1991. He could perhaps tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D32.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: There is a translation into the English language on the back, so 32A is the translation, and I tender this as evidence of the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I see a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document showing that the military command of Ilok has appointed me director of Agrokomerc in Ilok and on the 14th already I started working there in order to start production again, so that this would allow the city to function, because this included the bakery and other important points.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please continue about this visit of Slavko Dokmanovic and your place in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not seen Slavko Dokmanovic for a long time. He came to see me between 14 and 18 November. I remember it was morning. We said hello to each other. He told me why he had basically come. He said that he came in order to see whether Agrokomerc, as an enterprise could finance the overhaul which was in Backa Palanka in Napredak. I cannot even remember what the bill or how much money was involved. I said, "Slavko, I would be happy to do it, but we've just started working again and we don't have any money. If I can help you some other time, I would be happy to do so." We then talked a little bit and we complained to each other, and since we both had the labels we had, we did not dare go to Vukovar and we both, indeed, wanted to know what the situation was like there and what it was like, and it was even more difficult for him, because the accusations levelled against him were even graver -- people said he was a traitor, that he was a traitor, and this went from mouth to mouth. He really took it very hard. He asked me whether I knew some of these people in these different headquarters, did I know someone who could make it possible for him to go up there? I said; Slavko, I do not know them personally but I do not dare go myself, so I cannot do anything for you, either. We parted and after that we did not see each other for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since the military command even appointed directors of companies on the territory of the municipality of Vukovar, can we conclude that this entire territory was under military administration at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was a model that was unique to this entire area and this military command lasted longer, like in Ilok, and elsewhere, not that long, but it was the same model.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who governed Ilok after the war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also the military command from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the defence attorney please speak slower?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, how was Slavko Dokmanovic appointed Minister of Agriculture in the Government of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there at that election, but there were not very many eligible people around then. There were people who were all over, so he had training in agriculture, he was an agronomist, and he was really an expert in agricultural production, so he could have re-established this kind of production.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Vracaric, can you tell me, from the time that you left Vukovar -- which I think you said was in August -- until the date that you were appointed to this position in November 1991, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Backa Palanka as a refugee. I was staying with friends, and I had sent my children there already in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Backa Palanka is in Serbia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, near Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were there many Serb refugees there who had left Vukovar during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Backa Palanka, as in other towns along the Danube, there were truly quite a few refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when did you actually go to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Ilok some time before 1 November. I started coming to Ilok then, because the army allowed people to enter Ilok then and then I would go back to Backa Palanka -- I would commute. I definitely moved to Ilok the day I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to Ilok, did you find accommodation suitable for you to live in when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military command allow me to use a house on a temporary basis -- the house of a certain Mr. Vlado Zec, who had left Ilok in a convoy in October, together with the other inhabitants of Ilok .

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This gentleman that occupied this house, was he Croatian -- was he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec was a Croat and we met personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the time that you reached Ilok, most of the Croats had left, had they, or the vast majority of them had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the vast majority of Croats had left Ilok -- almost all the Slovaks had remained and a part of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the position that you had as Director of the company of Agrokomerc, if I have that correctly, what was the functions and duties that you performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My duties were, first and foremost, to resume production, because there was agricultural production there and also bread was baked and supplies were provided to the city and there was a metal production, too, so this was my primary duty and, secondly, I was supposed to get all the right people who would be in charge of this production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was under military command -- was this company under military command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All companies were under this command, and, during those first few days we would even submit reports to the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you wear a camouflage uniform when you were working for this company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never wore a camouflage uniform. The first day I reported in for work, I wore a suit and a tie and, later, this was given a negative connotation because most people moved around in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you said, "Most people moved around in military uniforms," were the people that were moving around in military uniforms -- were they all parts of the former JNA, or did people wear military uniforms, because it gave a favourable impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most people belonged to the JNA, or were reservists, and there were others, also, who wore at least part of a uniform, because this left a certain impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, it was quite popular for people to wear uniforms that appeared of a military nature -- they may not have necessarily been of any particular unit or formally part of the army, but it was quite popular, was it not, during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not compulsory to wear a uniform and there were different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. When you were in Backa Palanka, what were the conditions there like in terms of living conditions -- can you describe the conditions that you were living under?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many refugees -- Svetozar Jovic and later Stanko Jovic were the friends that I was staying with, and I lived under proper conditions -- these were wonderful people, because they really made me and my family feel at home, we practically did not pay for any of the expenses incurred except for what we spent on ourselves for personal things. In Palanka itself, there were truly very many people, like in Sid and all these other places -- some of them had a very hard life and others were better off depending on when they had come and with what.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is no question that conditions would have been tough for people who were there at that time, but apart from the inconvenience of having to be crowded in refugee circumstances, all the facilities were functioning, though, were they not, such as the electricity, water supply and things of that nature -- they were still functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was still functioning for those people who were staying with relatives and friends in privately owned houses. Others, who were staying at collective centres, had a tougher time. Of course, it is an automatic thing that life is more difficult under such circumstances, but it was not that people came of their own free will; it was a difficult situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned how you used to know Mr. Mercep and, as time progressed, he appeared to change. That was during the course of primarily 1991, was it, that this change occurred in Mr. Mercep that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mercep always had strong political ambitions. He always aspired to be a leader and, as time went by, he became increasingly impatient and increasingly aggressive. What I noticed about him was the following: he had bad people around him -- people of a suspicious status, people who were criminals, like Marko Obasic, the Dosen brothers and the like. I told him once, I said, "Tomica, can't you choose some better people to be around you? Why do you let these people come and stay with you?". He said, "These people suit me fine; they have nothing to lose."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that is true, is it not, of other people in the HDZ -- they went from being moderate and reasonable and fair, from your point of view, to a point of being much more extreme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the individual concerned. I mentioned, for example, Marin Vidic Bili -- he never changed into an extremist. As this euphoria grew, many of the moderates moved towards the extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think one of the reasons you have just mentioned a minute ago was the people he associated with, but you would agree with me, would you not, that a lot of these changes from people being moderate and having good and harmonious relations, to taking extreme positions -- much of that was brought about by the circumstances that were transpiring during the course of 1991 -- that is a fair statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what circumstances you have in mind. On our part, as Serbs, and members of the SDP club, we always sent positive signals and, as time went by, more and more negative signals were being sent to us. If these are the circumstances that you are referring to, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you knew Mr. Dokmanovic, and that you used to have meetings on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I presume from your statement you meant meetings during the course of the battle in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked to each other once or twice on the phone and once I met him when wheat was being purchased -- all of that was before the battle of Vukovar. Actually, could you please be more specific in terms of the date, because the battle of Vukovar did not take one day only, to the best of my knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, I am just relying on your statement and there is nothing specific about it there. It simply says in the last sentence: "We used to meet during the period in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I know that he never stayed in Vukovar during the war." It is only me assuming that you are talking about the time when he left and you had left Vukovar -- that is all I was asking you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the period before the real war operations in Vukovar. This was August/September -- I got out on 31 August, so it is that period -- September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nature of the meetings -- was this the Government of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem -- is that when you met with him -- when the Government was meeting -- is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. We would meet as friends, who talked on the phone -- let us get together -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see, fair enough. You mentioned also in your evidence that Mr. Dokmanovic approached you about a truck. Do you know what the truck was to be used for -- did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic was in charge of agriculture in Erdut, and he told me that it was a truck that was to be used for wheat or rape seed or something and that it broke down, and that they needed to have it repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the war, that is, during the month of December 1991, did you ever have occasion to go to Sremska Mitrovica by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Sremska Mitrovica in December -- no, not on business, nor do I know anyone there -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know a person with the same surname as yours, but with the first name Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a person who has the same surname as I do -- I think he had a car wash at the point where people entered Vukovar, on the right-hand side, before the war. We have the same surname, but we are not related.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a brief clarification. You were discussing the conditions under which refugees lived in Backa Palanka, which is on the territory of the Republic of Serbia. What were the conditions in the villages around Vukovar in that area, from the point of view of utilities, water, electricity and all the other indispensables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Vukovar, and I told you when, for as long as I could talk to my parents, who were in Vukovar -- in Vukovar it was worse and worse -- without electricity, without water -- as long as I could talk to my parents on the phone, they kept begging me to try to get them out of there, but I was not in a position to do so any more -- I know that the situation was bad in Vukovar itself. I did not go to the villages in the Vukovar municipality. Just like Dokmanovic, I was not too popular, so I could not really move around these villages and see what the conditions were like there, but it is true that people came en masse even from these homogenous villages that were Serb, predominantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have only one question. If I understood you correctly, you said that you were, between September and October 1991, in Backa Palanka, and then, as from 1 November or early November onwards in Ilok; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would come to Ilok in those days, because it was possible to get into Ilok -- I would come in and go out, go back to Backa Palanka and on 14 November I started working there, and that is when I worked in this house of Vlado Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand quite well whether, in this particular period September and November 1991, you actually met Mr. Dokmanovic, or only spoke with him on the phone -- I think you said that you phoned each other and then you also met as friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked to each other on the phone twice and once we met as friends, briefly, in Bac -- it was a very brief meeting -- we talked to each other, we complained to each other, and then we parted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When did this meeting take place -- this meeting in Bac, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bac, I think we met some time in September -- mid September -- the end of September -- I really cannot recall -- I cannot be sure on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you remember how Mr. Dokmanovic was dressed? Was he wearing a suit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just like I was dressed -- in jeans and a sweater with -- civilian clothes just like I was wearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No further questions. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Thank you so much for coming. You may now be released. We still have half an hour. We should start with the next witness. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Kresojevic -- I think he will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might we get an indication from the defence which witnesses they are calling next week and in what order? I think things have changed a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If we get through the testimony of Mr. Kresojevic today, and it is not left over for next week, the first witness will be an expert witness,(redacted). After him, we expect (redacted)Ljubomar Novakovic and Dragutin Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we expect him, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It will be six.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Five -- Antic will not be coming -- let me repeat, Bulajic, Antic, Novakovic (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Novakovic is not coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Novakovic -- again, Bulajic first; Antic; Novakovic (redacted) 14 (redacted)-- the order is not the same order as you have on the list, but those are the names of the witnesses who shall be coming. RADIVOJE KRESOJEVIC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Examination-in-chief by MR. PETROVIC:

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
