utterances.text: Mr. Kresojevic, just briefly, where did you go to school, what qualifications do you have, and your place of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primary school, I completed in my native village of Bobota, secondary school in Vukovar, I went to the higher agricultural school in Vinkovski and afterwards did my military service in the JNA. On 1 July 1979 I started working in the Vukovar Vupik Cooperation in Bobota.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you first get to know Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Slavko Dokmanovic in the 1970s, at football matches between my village of Bobota and his native village of Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You were elected a deputy for the Municipal Assembly at the multi-Party elections. Could you tell us of the constitution of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar and the election of President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the first multi-Party elections in the Republic of Croatia, the Serb people did not have their National Party -- the only option at the time was the SDP, that is to say, the former Party of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was the Municipal Assembly constituted after the local elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly, after the elections, and the SDP/SKH was victorious, in such a way as the committee of the SKH and SDP, together with the deputies elected in the Assembly, put forward Slavko Dokmanovic for President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how did the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar function in those first months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the work of the Municipal Assembly was correct -- the professional services, which Mr. Dokmanovic led, prepared all the joint sessions of all three Chambers of the Municipal Assembly. The material, the documents for the Municipal Assembly was given to us 10 to 15 days earlier, with an agenda so that I think that everything evolved according to the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you assess the work of Slavko Dokmanovic as the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic as President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar demonstrated a considerable tolerance, peace loving qualities, patience in solving very important and burning issues of the kind that came up before the Assembly, and in the region of the municipality of Vukovar, especially as the members of the HDZ were not pleased to see the victory of the SDP Party and could not accept this peacefully, and organised excessive situations so as to upset the work of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did some circles among the Serb population react to this conciliatory policy waged by the President of the Municipal Assembly at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Serb population did not like the conduct of the President and its own deputies representing them in the Municipal Assembly, because apparent authority at this level was shared with the HDZ. They even received more positions of leadership than would other be accorded them on the basis of their electoral results, so they were bitter. At one particular moment, we experienced the fact that our compatriots told us that we were waging a policy which was geared towards turning over power to the HDZ peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the Municipal Assembly cease to perform its functions in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17 May 1991, an Assembly meeting was convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why was it not held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not held because the extremists, the activists and deputies of the HDZ, even stopped the members from coming even by resorting to arms, so they were not able to come to this regularly convened Municipal Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were the deputies searched upon entry into the building of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a group of people, some 500 of them had collected in front of the building and, when I came, they used insulting language -- insults were hurled at the Serb people. We did not allow ourselves to be searched and, quite simply, myself, together with Mr. Juros Ivan, who was a SABOR deputy, we went in the direction of the courtyard of Vupik from Vukovar, took an official vehicle and returned to Bobota.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After 17 May 1991 did you return to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 17 May 1991 I did not return to Vukovar, because barricades were erected at the cafe bar Cirih at the entry to Vukovar and I did not allow myself or my family to go to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who held the barricades at the Cirih cafe bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was held by the HDZ members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the villages around Vukovar, what were the conditions of living -- was there any water, electricity and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the villages -- Vukovar and its environs, at that time, in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, were highly developed -- it was an environment in which a lot was being done, and the results of that work going on were the material goods that the individual households had, so that, in a way, people had some reserves, and they did not have any problems with maintaining the livelihood of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they have electricity in that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during that time they did have electricity, but later on there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the Municipal Assembly formally cease to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a deputy, I did not receive any official information that the Assembly had ceased to work, but, through the media, I learned that the Government of the Republic of Croatia had replaced Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic and that Mr. Vidic had been appointed and that the Assembly had dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After the war activities in Vukovar, was there any civilian authority on the territory of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian power and authority did not exist -- there was military rule, together with a crisis headquarters in the local communities, and, if you wanted to go from the area of the municipality, you would have to get a permit to do so in the headquarters, and then you would go to the headquarters in Vukovar to be able to move into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There were watch points as well, checkpoints, and several military commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the first organs of civilian power -- when were they formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in December, the beginning of December, I think, because of the burgeoning problems, which the armed conflicts brought with them and in Vukovar an Executive Council was set up, led by Mr. Rajko Bibic and seven of his associates for the individual departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was Slavko Dokmanovic elected President of the Municipal Assembly for the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first elections which took place in our area -- there are elections in the Serb Krajina region -- political life had been revived, so that, at that particular time, there were a number of parties and different options -- parties that had their programmes in the pre-election campaign. You had the Serb Democratic Party, the Serb Radical Party and the Serb Party of Socialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you just tell us finally whether on 8 January (INAUDIBLE) you had talks with Miroslav Vasic, the investigator, and whether you made a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement? I tender it in the Serb original and the English translation. I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D33, English translation D33A. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, are you tendering this in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am tendering it in evidence -- D33 and 33A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, or rather, good afternoon, Mr. Kresojevic. I am Stefan Waespi appearing for the Prosecution in this case and I have a number of questions to you. Can you tell the court, please, where you were living exactly in the summer or fall of 1991 -- in a village, in a town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Bobota, in my native village. On 15 November 1991, I went to Belgrade to have an operation -- I returned from the operation somewhere at the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, besides about these maybe two weeks in November 1991, you were always living in the village of Bobota, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this village is about 10 kilometres north-west of Vukovar, of the city of Vukovar; is that also a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it is 10 or 15, but around there -- 10 to 15, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And one of the neighbouring villages in fact is the village of Trpinja -- is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that electricity functioned normally throughout a certain time and you said it went away or it was cut off. Can you specify a date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact date, but it was somewhere in August -- some time in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for how long was it like this -- what could you tell us -- was it only a brief interruption or was it going on without electricity for months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several months, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it reinstalled in the same year in 1991, or only in the following year? If you are not sure, it has been seven years or more -- it was just sort of several months you said it was cut off, at least, the electricity, that is what you are saying, but you do not really know exactly when it was cut off and when it was resumed -- is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly when it was reinstalled -- I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That is fine. How about water and other utilities -- people survived -- you survived, fortunately, but there was some water, obviously, for the population -- at least you can only testify for your village, in the village of Bobota, is that correct, that there was water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The waterworks in Bobota is based on electricity, so when there is no electricity, there is no water, either. For the village's needs, we were given aggregates, which was switched on, and they worked for three to four hours a day, which meant that the population had enough water during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, what you are saying is that, even the cut-off of the normal supply, the daily pre-war supply of electricity, there were instances where you really had electricity -- of course, for the purposes only for emergency situations or needs like getting the water pumps to work -- is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no electricity, no light, but, as I say, the waterworks did function through an aggregate which allowed enough supplies of water for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you knew Mr. Dokmanovic through sport in the 1970s and I think you mentioned, also, that you were playing football with each other or against each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Opposite teams, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many times did you meet Mr. Dokmanovic in those days before the end of the war in Vukovar -- before the final days of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Bobota, as I said, some time around 15 November. Before that, we met on several occasions, but always -- as I was the leader of the cooperation department in Bobota, and an agricultural engineer, Mr. Dokmanovic, was an agronomist, an agricultural expert as well, so we met in that capacity, and to discuss the wheat harvest, soya, sunflower harvest, maze and so on and so forth -- because our region is a farming region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these several occasions you were meeting Mr. Dokmanovic, do you remember what he was wearing -- a uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that, as we followed the work of the combine harvesters and the machines, we sometimes used track suits or sports footwear -- we did not -- we were not in any military formations, so we did not have any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How about yourself -- you also switched between civilian clothes and uniforms in these times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, we did not belong to any military formations and, because of the situation that we experienced after the work of the Municipal Assembly, we were given the assignments of working in the field of agriculture and not any military jobs, because they had proclaimed us traitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that reflected in the way you were dressed, given assignments of working in the field of agriculture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, our working uniform, that is, the usual type of clothing for the heads of departments -- no military uniform -- it was a normal civilian type of uniform that we used when we went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. After the war, or after the end of the battle of Vukovar, did you see Mr. Dokmanovic again -- perhaps when you returned from hospital in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I returned from the hospital in Belgrade, I spent some time, that is to say, I did not have any duties to perform, even professionally, within my profession, that is to say, agriculture. It was only in spring or in the summer, actually, when I took up my duties in the cooperative once again, and I met Mr. Dokmanovic on several occasions as the Minister of Agriculture, or the man responsible for agricultural problems in the area that we covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned that incident -- I think it was on 17 May 1991, when you and other members of the Assembly were not allowed to enter the building. Do you think it is correct to say that you should not wear any weapons inside a parliamentary building -- would you agree with me on that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The deputies did not have to, nor did they have any need to, wear any weapons. I did not have any -- I never had occasion to fear anyone, because I lived in my native village, and my native town, so to speak, where I knew many people and I never felt -- I still did not feel the need to wear any weapons, for the simple reason that the police -- to give the police at the time an argument against us, that is to say, deputies who did not agree with policy, so I never saw any of the SDP members carrying any weapons to an assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, since there was some tension -- you have described in your testimony -- in those months, it is probably quite prudent of any formations or police to make sure that none of the politicians who would go to a meeting would be armed -- would you agree with that? I am not suggesting that you were armed, but just to make sure that nobody would enter that building with any arms -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building of the Municipal Assembly and in front of the building, on that particular day, 17 May, members and sympathisers of the HDZ were seen with pistols, that is to say, with weapons. I, as a man who never thought of taking part in the war -- I am opposed to any kind of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I completely agree with you. I am just making the statement that it would be reasonable that Assembly members of any type of Party -- I am not saying which ones -- that they are searched in the times you have just described before they enter the parliamentary building. I am suggesting, or I wonder whether you would agree with me to say that it was correct that these people are searched before they enter the building, or would you say that it is unreasonable to search the members of the Parliament before they enter the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I perhaps came a little later -- perhaps I came to the Municipal Assembly building later, when this mass of people had already gathered. I was not searched and I would not allow them to search me, because I saw that they were prohibiting entry into the building, so I just turned around and went back to where I came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have no questions. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned and we start again on Monday, at 8.30 sharp. (At 1.16 p.m. the matter adjourned until Monday, 27 April 1998, at 8.30 a.m.) 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
